\chapter{What is SCRIMP?}
\label{\detokenize{index:what-is-scrimp}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{SCRIMP} (Simulation and ContRol of Interactions in Multi\sphinxhyphen{}Physics) is a python collection, \sphinxstyleemphasis{namely} a package, of \sphinxstyleemphasis{methods} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{classes} for the structure\sphinxhyphen{}preserving discretization and simulation of multi\sphinxhyphen{}physics models, using the formalism of port\sphinxhyphen{}Hamiltonian systems (\sphinxhref{https://doi.org/10.1016/S0393-0440(01)00083-3}{van der Schaft and Maschke (2002)}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{SCRIMP} aims at speeding the coding process of the \sphinxstylestrong{Partitioned Finite Element Method} on a wide range of (multi\sphinxhyphen{})physical systems (\sphinxhref{https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ifacol.2024.08.267}{Ferraro *et al.* (2024)}), and scrimp and save time!

\sphinxAtStartPar
The documentation is \sphinxhref{https://g-haine.github.io/scrimp/latex/scrimp.pdf}{available in pdf}.


\section{Port\sphinxhyphen{}Hamiltonian systems}
\label{\detokenize{index:port-hamiltonian-systems}}

\subsection{What are they?}
\label{\detokenize{index:what-are-they}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let us sketch a rough portrait of port\sphinxhyphen{}Hamiltonian systems as they are considered in \sphinxstylestrong{SCRIMP}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Port\sphinxhyphen{}Hamiltonian systems constitute a strongly structured class of control systems with collocated observation. It relies on a functional form \(\mathcal{H}\) (the \sphinxstylestrong{Hamiltonian}), whose variables \(\alpha_i\) are the \sphinxstylestrong{states} of the system. The \sphinxstylestrong{co\sphinxhyphen{}states} \(M_i e_i := \delta_{\alpha_i} \mathcal{H}\) are defined as the variational derivative of the Hamiltonian with respect to the states, on the metric induced by the \(M_i\) matrices.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The dynamics is provided \sphinxstyleemphasis{via} trajectories belonging in a \sphinxstylestrong{Dirac} structure, which can be represented by two matrices (of operators) \(M\) symmetric and \(J\) skew\sphinxhyphen{}symmetric as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}M
\begin{pmatrix} \frac{\rm d}{{\rm d}t} \alpha_1(t) \\ \vdots \\ \frac{\rm d}{{\rm d}t} \alpha_k(t) \\ f_R(t) \\ - y_{exp}(t) \\ u_{imp}(t) \end{pmatrix}
= J
\begin{pmatrix} e_1(t) \\ \vdots \\ e_k(t) \\ e_R(t) \\ u_{exp}(t) \\ - y_{imp}(t) \end{pmatrix}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
together with \sphinxstylestrong{constitutive relations}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}M_i e_i(t) = \delta_{\alpha_i(t)} \mathcal{H}(\alpha_1(t), \cdots, \alpha_k(t))
\qquad
\mathcal{N}(t, f_R(t), e_R(t)) = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This structure allows to describe the evolution of the Hamiltonian along the trajectories
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{\rm d}{{\rm d}t} \mathcal{H}(\alpha_1(t), \cdots, \alpha_k(t)) = - e_R(t)^\top M_R f_R(t) + u_{exp}(t)^\top M_{exp} y_{exp}(t) + u_{imp}(t)^\top M_{imp} y_{imp}(t)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The first term of the right\sphinxhyphen{}hand side stands for a loss of \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy}, hence the name of \sphinxstyleemphasis{resistive (or dissipative) port} for the couple \((f_R,e_R)\). The other two terms stands for exchanges with the environment through the \sphinxstyleemphasis{control ports}. One is \sphinxstyleemphasis{explicit}, \(u_{exp}\), as a usual forcing term in the equations (its collocated output \(y_{exp}\) plays no role in the dynamics). The other is \sphinxstyleemphasis{implicit}: \(u_{imp}\) does not appear directly in the dynamics, and its collocated output \(y_{imp}\) plays the role of the Lagrange multiplier imposing the value of \(u_{imp}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each indexed matrix \(M_\ell\) is the appropriate sub\sphinxhyphen{}matrix of \(M\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
A very important and useful fact is that the matrices \(M\) and \(J\) can depend on time and states!


\subsection{The Partitioned Finite Element Method}
\label{\detokenize{index:the-partitioned-finite-element-method}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The main objective of a \sphinxstylestrong{structure\sphinxhyphen{}preserving discretization} in the port\sphinxhyphen{}Hamiltonian formalism is to obtain a discrete version of the power balance satisfied by the Hamiltonian functional.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A recent scheme, known as the \sphinxstylestrong{Partitioned Finite Element Method} (PFEM) (\sphinxhref{https://doi.org/10.1093/imamci/dnaa038}{Cardoso\sphinxhyphen{}Ribeiro *et al.* (2021)}), achieves this goal.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The strategy follows three steps, inspired by the Mixed Finite Element Method for steady\sphinxhyphen{}state problem with homogeneous boundary condition
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
write the weak form of the system;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
integrate by parts a \sphinxstylestrong{partition} of the state (such that \sphinxstyleemphasis{the control appears}); and

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
project on finite element spaces.

\end{itemize}


\section{Coding philosophy}
\label{\detokenize{index:coding-philosophy}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{SCRIMP} assumes that the final user is not familiar with numerical simulations. The aim is to facilitate the first step from modelisation to simulation by sticking as much as possible to the port\sphinxhyphen{}Hamiltonian framework, getting rid of coding issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As such, these simplifications naturally imply a lack of optimization of the code. Nevertheless, the syntax of \sphinxstylestrong{SCRIMP} try to let confirmed users to reach finer tuning in order to perform more sophisticated simulations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A basic usage of \sphinxstylestrong{SCRIMP} consists in a script with the following steps:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a \sphinxstyleemphasis{domain}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define at least one \sphinxstyleemphasis{state}. And of course, its \sphinxstyleemphasis{co\sphinxhyphen{}state}, in order to get a \sphinxstyleemphasis{dynamical port}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Choose a spatial Finite Element Method for a distributed port, or use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{add\_lumped\_port}} for a global scalar port (one degree of freedom)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define \sphinxstyleemphasis{algebraic ports} (not mandatory) and its FEM

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define \sphinxstyleemphasis{control ports} (not mandatory) and its FEM

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define \sphinxstyleemphasis{parameters}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Write down the forms on the \sphinxstyleemphasis{flow side} of the Dirac structure, \sphinxstyleemphasis{i.e.} the \sphinxstylestrong{brick} defining the matrix \(M\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Write down the forms on the \sphinxstyleemphasis{effort side} of the Dirac structure, \sphinxstyleemphasis{i.e.} th \sphinxstylestrong{brick} defining the matrix \(J\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Write down all the forms defining the \sphinxstyleemphasis{constitutive relations}, always with \sphinxstylestrong{bricks}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Set up time scheme options: again, at first glance, default values are sufficient

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Solve

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Plot

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Export

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
We try to eliminate as much as possible the \sphinxstyleemphasis{computer\sphinxhyphen{}side} of the simulations, by following the port\sphinxhyphen{}Hamiltonian vocabulary, always by keeping the possibility of fine tuning available.


\chapter{User’s guide}
\label{\detokenize{index:user-s-guide}}
\sphinxstepscope


\section{How to install}
\label{\detokenize{install:how-to-install}}\label{\detokenize{install::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Docker is the recommended/default installation for SCRIMP v1.3.0.}
The published Linux/AMD64 image provides a precompiled environment
containing Python, GetFEM 5.5, PETSc/SLEPc (complex), MUMPS, OpenMPI and
SCRIMP itself. User simulations and their outputs live in an
\sphinxstylestrong{independent, host\sphinxhyphen{}owned project}, not inside the image or a SCRIMP
source checkout. A source checkout is \sphinxstylestrong{not} needed by a released\sphinxhyphen{}image
user.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{important}{Important:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{SCRIMP v1.3.0 (27 November 2026):} the stable Git tag and
\sphinxstylestrong{public} \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ghcr.io/g\sphinxhyphen{}haine/scrimp:1.3.0}} Docker image are available.
The stable image retains the accepted \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dist\sphinxhyphen{}rc4}} OCI index digest
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sha256:737f58f12475723c0924f25528a0794a767fe6051dbecbd80a194d3b15eb3f01}}
and was built from Git revision
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{17ae5a1ce063ff5481812dc73f3d3fc88c153c70}}.
A fresh Ubuntu 24.04/AMD64 runner validated the independent user
project/host CSV, MPI startup and native Heat\textendash{}Wave Hamiltonian
parity (\sphinxhref{https://github.com/g-haine/scrimp/actions/runs/46030753404}{CI evidence}).
The standalone user ZIP is distributed separately through the
\sphinxhref{https://github.com/g-haine/scrimp/releases/tag/v1.3.0}{v1.3.0 GitHub Release}.
Windows/macOS/ARM64 remain best\sphinxhyphen{}effort.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Default: precompiled Docker and standalone project}
\label{\detokenize{install:default-precompiled-docker-and-standalone-project}}\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Install Docker (on Windows, Docker Desktop with WSL2; on macOS,
Docker Desktop). VS Code and Dev Containers are recommended for
editing/debugging but \sphinxstylestrong{not required} for command\sphinxhyphen{}line execution.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Download the matching
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scrimp\sphinxhyphen{}project\sphinxhyphen{}template.zip}} asset from the SCRIMP v1.3.0
GitHub Release and unpack it into your own project directory. The
release ZIP embeds the \sphinxstylestrong{validated} image reference in
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.devcontainer/devcontainer.json}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pull the released Docker image:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
docker\PYG{+w}{ }pull\PYG{+w}{ }ghcr.io/g\PYGZhy{}haine/scrimp:1.3.0
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Open the project directory in VS Code and choose
\sphinxstylestrong{Dev Containers: Reopen in Container}. In its terminal, run:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
python\PYG{+w}{ }simulations/first\PYGZus{}simulation.py
mpiexec\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }python\PYG{+w}{ }simulations/mpi\PYGZus{}check.py
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The oscillator is a real serial SCRIMP simulation and saves
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{outputs/oscillator.csv}} \sphinxstylestrong{on the host}. The second command
checks only MPI startup, not a distributed PDE power/physics result.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Without VS Code, execute the same project by mounting your
independent workspace (Linux shell):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZti{}/MySCRIMPProject
docker\PYG{+w}{ }run\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}rm\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}user\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{k}{\PYGZdl{}(}id\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}u\PYG{k}{)}\PYG{l+s+s2}{:}\PYG{k}{\PYGZdl{}(}id\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}g\PYG{k}{)}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYGZhy{}e\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{HOME}\PYG{o}{=}/tmp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}e\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{XDG\PYGZus{}CACHE\PYGZus{}HOME}\PYG{o}{=}/tmp/.cache\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYGZhy{}v\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}PWD}\PYG{l+s+s2}{:/work:rw}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}w\PYG{+w}{ }/work\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }ghcr.io/g\PYGZhy{}haine/scrimp:1.3.0\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }python\PYG{+w}{ }simulations/first\PYGZus{}simulation.py
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
On Docker Desktop, permissions and mount semantics differ; consult
the Windows/macOS guidance below. No numerical output belongs
in a throwaway container filesystem.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The complete standalone workspace, release ZIP generation, explicit
image tags and F5 debugging are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{vscode::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{First SCRIMP project with VS Code (v1.3.0)}}}}.
The distribution qualification contract (including exact source
revision, image metadata, host CSV and MPI tests) is documented
in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{docs/V130\_DOCKER\_FIRST\_RELEASE\_GATE.md}}. All required
Linux/AMD64 distribution checks have passed; that does not
qualify other platforms.


\subsection{Alternative: native Conda installation}
\label{\detokenize{install:alternative-native-conda-installation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The original Conda workflow is retained for current users and
advanced developers. It is \sphinxstylestrong{not} the v1.3.0 default.
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Install \sphinxhref{https://docs.conda.io/}{Conda} or
\sphinxhref{https://mamba.readthedocs.io/}{Micromamba}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Clone the repository: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{git clone https://github.com/g\sphinxhyphen{}haine/scrimp}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Enter the folder: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cd scrimp}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Run \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{conda env create \sphinxhyphen{}f scrimp.yml}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Activate: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{conda activate scrimp}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Install SCRIMP: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{python \sphinxhyphen{}m pip install \sphinxhyphen{}e .}}.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The historical \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scrimp.yml}} deliberately retains its older
packaged GetFEM/NumPy dependencies for existing users; \sphinxstylestrong{do not}
interpret native Conda as a validated GetFEM 5.5/MPI/NumPy 2
replacement for the candidate Docker stack.


\subsection{Modern parallel Docker image (GetFEM 5.5)}
\label{\detokenize{install:modern-parallel-docker-image-getfem-5-5}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The v1.3.0 \sphinxstylestrong{Docker build} recipe is in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{docker/Dockerfile}},
with dependencies in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{docker/environment.yml}}. It uses one
consistent conda\sphinxhyphen{}forge OpenMPI stack and complex PETSc/SLEPc/MUMPS.
The PETSc/SLEPc Python bindings are compiled against the installed
native libraries and NumPy 2 headers. GetFEM 5.5 is compiled with
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}enable\sphinxhyphen{}paralevel=2}}, including SCRIMP’s approved simplex
BDM/Nédélec source patches.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Native dependencies are now compiled in \sphinxstylestrong{cache\sphinxhyphen{}friendly layers
before copying SCRIMP’s Python sources}. Docker BuildKit retains
APT, Micromamba, pip and verified GetFEM tarball downloads.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The candidate build driver fetches the selected GitHub revision
by default into a temporary checkout and stages only audited tracked
sources in a \sphinxstyleemphasis{second} isolated context. It \sphinxstylestrong{never hands Docker the
live SCRIMP repository}, even if the user has tens of gigabytes
of simulations under sandbox/outputs. For intentionally local
library development, set \sphinxtitleref{SCRIMP\_DOCKER\_SOURCE=local}; this still
copies only tracked allowlisted source files into the build context.
Neither mode includes user simulation data.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use an \sphinxstylestrong{independently tagged candidate}, not the qualified existing
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scrimp\sphinxhyphen{}mpi:local}} image:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZti{}/Simulations/scrimp
git\PYG{+w}{ }pull\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}ff\PYGZhy{}only
bash\PYG{+w}{ }scripts/build\PYGZhy{}v130\PYGZhy{}docker\PYGZhy{}candidate.sh
bash\PYG{+w}{ }scripts/smoke\PYGZhy{}v130\PYGZhy{}docker\PYGZhy{}candidate.sh
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
By default these target \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scrimp\sphinxhyphen{}mpi:v1.3.0\sphinxhyphen{}rc1}}. The build script
writes \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sandbox/outputs/v130\sphinxhyphen{}docker\sphinxhyphen{}build.log}} and records the
built image ID; the smoke writes
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sandbox/outputs/v130\sphinxhyphen{}docker\sphinxhyphen{}smoke.log}}, exports the exact
resolved Conda package spec and checks the GetFEM simplex descriptor
support, NumPy ABI, complex PETSc and distributed MUMPS at 1/2 ranks.
It explicitly rejects Nédélec\sphinxhyphen{}II order k\textgreater{}=3, which has \sphinxstylestrong{not}
been implemented.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rc1}} script default is a \sphinxstylestrong{local development candidate tag},
not the public image. To use the stable qualified environment,
pull \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ghcr.io/g\sphinxhyphen{}haine/scrimp:1.3.0}} instead. Do not overwrite a
validated local image while experimenting with source builds.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For interactive development with an \sphinxstylestrong{independent local
simulation project} (not the source checkout), see {\hyperref[\detokenize{vscode::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{First SCRIMP project with VS Code (v1.3.0)}}}}.
For a manual command\sphinxhyphen{}line session from the user’s simulation folder:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZti{}/MySCRIMPProject
sudo\PYG{+w}{ }docker\PYG{+w}{ }run\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}rm\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}it\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}v\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}PWD}\PYG{l+s+s2}{:/work}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}workdir\PYG{+w}{ }/work\PYG{+w}{ }ghcr.io/g\PYGZhy{}haine/scrimp:1.3.0\PYG{+w}{ }bash
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This binds the local workspace read\sphinxhyphen{}write, so simulations and outputs
persist on the host even when the container is removed. On Linux,
check UID/GID mapping before relying on direct docker\sphinxhyphen{}run commands;
the VS Code Dev Containers template enables UID matching.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Further instructions and the cache\sphinxhyphen{}validation protocol are in
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{docs/V130\_DOCKER\_BUILD.md}}. The stable image is publicly available as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ghcr.io/g\sphinxhyphen{}haine/scrimp:1.3.0}}.
Existing Sphinx/Conda instructions for the stable \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scrimp.yml}}
environment remain unchanged.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The GitHub Actions workflow \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.github/workflows/docker\sphinxhyphen{}mpi.yml}}
is still manual\sphinxhyphen{}only and separately checks MPI/native assembly,
algebra and representative wave physics. GHCR publication remains
opt\sphinxhyphen{}in and must follow actual image validation; the local candidate
build script never publishes.


\subsection{Windows and macOS users: best\sphinxhyphen{}effort Docker/Dev Containers}
\label{\detokenize{install:windows-and-macos-users-best-effort-docker-dev-containers}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
SCRIMP has users on Windows and macOS. These are \sphinxstylestrong{best\sphinxhyphen{}effort
installation workflows}, not independently qualified native
Windows/macOS GetFEM/PETSc/MUMPS configurations. The released
Linux/AMD64 image is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ghcr.io/g\sphinxhyphen{}haine/scrimp:1.3.0}}.
Check its platform before use; historical local tags like
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scrimp\sphinxhyphen{}mpi:v1.3.0\sphinxhyphen{}rc3}} are not published GHCR tags.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Windows 10/11 (WSL2):} install Docker Desktop, enable its WSL2
backend and integration for your Linux distribution, and install
VS Code plus the Dev Containers extension. Open a \sphinxstylestrong{WSL2 Linux}
terminal and verify \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{docker version}}. Keep your SCRIMP user
project under the WSL2 Linux filesystem (rather than an NTFS
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/mnt/c}} mount) if you will create many numerical outputs.
From this terminal, after pulling a compatible image, run:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZti{}/MySCRIMPProject
docker\PYG{+w}{ }images
docker\PYG{+w}{ }run\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}rm\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}v\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}PWD}\PYG{l+s+s2}{:/work}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}w\PYG{+w}{ }/work\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }ghcr.io/g\PYGZhy{}haine/scrimp:1.3.0\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }python\PYG{+w}{ }simulations/first\PYGZus{}simulation.py
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These commands run a Linux container through WSL2; they do \sphinxstylestrong{not}
constitute a native Windows compilation. If Docker Desktop’s
integration/permissions differ, use its documented WSL2 integration
settings. Use {\hyperref[\detokenize{vscode::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{First SCRIMP project with VS Code (v1.3.0)}}}} for the independent project workflow.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{macOS (Intel/Apple Silicon):} install Docker Desktop for the
machine architecture and VS Code/Dev Containers. Once an image
exists locally, inspect its architecture using
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{docker image inspect IMAGE:TAG}}; a Linux AMD64\sphinxhyphen{}only image
will not become ARM64\sphinxhyphen{}native merely because Docker Desktop
can start it with emulation. On an Apple Silicon machine,
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}platform linux/amd64}} is a possible \sphinxstylestrong{experimental}
compatibility option for an AMD64 image, but its numerical
performance and GetFEM/PETSc/MUMPS MPI behavior remain unqualified:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZti{}/MySCRIMPProject
docker\PYG{+w}{ }run\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}rm\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}platform\PYG{+w}{ }linux/amd64\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYGZhy{}v\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}PWD}\PYG{l+s+s2}{:/work}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}w\PYG{+w}{ }/work\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }ghcr.io/g\PYGZhy{}haine/scrimp:1.3.0\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }python\PYG{+w}{ }simulations/first\PYGZus{}simulation.py
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Do not infer scientific accuracy or MPI safety from a successful
container launch. Prefer a separately built and validated ARM64
image when one becomes available. Docker Desktop’s bind\sphinxhyphen{}mount
permissions and filesystem performance differ from native Linux.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In \sphinxstylestrong{all} cases, begin with the bundled oscillator and a bounded
two\sphinxhyphen{}rank MPI start\sphinxhyphen{}up check, then progress to validated PDE models.
If your setup differs from the tested Linux baseline, record image
digest/platform, Python/PETSc/GetFEM versions and raw logs when
reporting a problem. Windows/macOS use is welcome, but it is
\sphinxstylestrong{not a mandatory v1.3.0 release\sphinxhyphen{}blocking acceptance gate}.


\subsection{Local GetFEM 5.5 MPI compilation (Conda environment)}
\label{\detokenize{install:local-getfem-5-5-mpi-compilation-conda-environment}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This approach enables a source build without Docker and keeps a
separate, isolated environment instead of modifying your existing
SCRIMP installation:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Ubuntu: GL runtime for the Gmsh Python wheel.}
sudo\PYG{+w}{ }apt\PYGZhy{}get\PYG{+w}{ }update
sudo\PYG{+w}{ }apt\PYGZhy{}get\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}y\PYG{+w}{ }binutils\PYG{+w}{ }file\PYG{+w}{ }libglu1\PYGZhy{}mesa\PYG{+w}{ }libgl1

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Create a new environment from the same solver\PYGZhy{}compatible recipe.}
conda\PYG{+w}{ }env\PYG{+w}{ }create\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }scrimp55\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }docker/environment.yml
conda\PYG{+w}{ }activate\PYG{+w}{ }scrimp55

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Build matching NumPy\PYGZhy{}2 Python wrappers against the installed}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} complex native PETSc/SLEPc (conda petsc4py may require NumPy\PYGZlt{}2).}
bash\PYG{+w}{ }scripts/install\PYGZhy{}petsc\PYGZhy{}python\PYGZhy{}bindings.sh

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Compile the official GetFEM 5.5 sources in MPI level 2.}
\PYG{n+nv}{GETFEM\PYGZus{}VERSION}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m}{5}.5\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{MAKE\PYGZus{}JOBS}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }bash\PYG{+w}{ }scripts/build\PYGZhy{}getfem\PYGZhy{}mpi.sh

python\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}m\PYG{+w}{ }pip\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}no\PYGZhy{}deps\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}no\PYGZhy{}build\PYGZhy{}isolation\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}e\PYG{+w}{ }.
python\PYG{+w}{ }sandbox/smoke\PYGZus{}modern\PYGZus{}stack.py
mpiexec\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }python\PYG{+w}{ }sandbox/smoke\PYGZus{}modern\PYGZus{}stack.py
mpiexec\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }python\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}m\PYG{+w}{ }unittest\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}v\PYG{+w}{ }tests.test\PYGZus{}mpi\PYGZus{}algebra
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The build script uses the active \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CONDA\_PREFIX}}, the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpicc/mpicxx/mpifort}} wrappers and a local build directory
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.build/getfem}}. It refuses to silently install a serial
GetFEM: it checks the runtime value
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{getfem.util\_mpi\_parallelism\_level() == 2}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Python 3.12 installation compatibility:} The GetFEM 5.5 tarball
still bundles an older Automake \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{py\sphinxhyphen{}compile}} that imports
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{imp}}, which was removed from Python 3.12. The shared
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scripts/build\sphinxhyphen{}getfem\sphinxhyphen{}mpi.sh}} installation therefore overrides
\sphinxstylestrong{only} Automake’s bytecode compiler
(\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make install \textquotesingle{}am\_\_py\_compile=:\textquotesingle{}}}), and immediately performs
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{compileall}} with the active Python interpreter. This retains
native build and installation, rather than downgrading Python
or installing a global \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{imp}} shim.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To build the latest \sphinxstylestrong{development} GetFEM, use
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GETFEM\_SOURCE=git GETFEM\_REF=\textless{}commit\sphinxhyphen{}sha\textgreater{}}} and keep the
specific upstream commit in the experiment manifest.
That is separate from the stable \sphinxstylestrong{5.5 release}. The tarball
checksum may be pinned through \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GETFEM\_SHA256}}; this
must be set when turning an experimental recipe into a
reproducible release.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{NumPy 2 compatibility} is currently a validation goal, not
an asserted upstream guarantee. The C extension must be compiled
against the NumPy 2 headers in the environment and tested at
runtime. If either compilation or tests fail, do not downgrade
NumPy silently inside the modern environment; preserve the
error logs for debugging. Keep \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scrimp.yml}} as a fallback.


\subsection{Native GetFEM MPI assembly timing verbosity}
\label{\detokenize{install:native-getfem-mpi-assembly-timing-verbosity}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
GetFEM 5.5 prints \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Assembly time ...}} for \sphinxstylestrong{every model assembly}
on the master MPI rank, even when SCRIMP calls
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gf.util\_trace\_level(0)}}. This comes from an unconditional
C++ \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{std::cout}} in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/getfem\_models.cc}}, rather than
SCRIMP’s Python logger.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstylestrong{new native GetFEM builds made with SCRIMP’s build script},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scripts/patches/getfem\sphinxhyphen{}5.5/0000\sphinxhyphen{}mpi\sphinxhyphen{}assembly\sphinxhyphen{}timing.patch}} changes
only this diagnostic print, after extracting the upstream source and
before compilation. It is applied by the same ordered patch loop as
the BDM fix. Normal execution is quiet. To restore upstream\sphinxhyphen{}style
per\sphinxhyphen{}assembly timing information for diagnosis, set:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nv}{SCRIMP\PYGZus{}GETFEM\PYGZus{}ASSEMBLY\PYGZus{}TIMING}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }mpiexec\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }python\PYG{+w}{ }sandbox/smoke\PYGZus{}modern\PYGZus{}stack.py
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The flag must be present in the environment \sphinxstylestrong{inside} the
container and on all MPI ranks. The source patch fails to apply if
GetFEM’s expected code has changed: it must be reviewed rather than
silently forced. Neither mathematical expressions, assembly results,
nor MPI communication are changed. Avoid silencing all stdout/stderr
in Python: GetFEM’s native errors and diagnostics must remain visible.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{An image built before this change still prints the messages.}
Rebuilding the native GetFEM layer is necessary to change that image;
defer it to the next planned image rebuild rather than recompiling
GetFEM solely to remove cosmetic output.


\subsection{Native GetFEM MPI assembly audit (important)}
\label{\detokenize{install:native-getfem-mpi-assembly-audit-important}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Before interpreting any parallel simulation, compare the \sphinxstylestrong{raw
GetFEM outputs} at P=1, 2 and 4. The official GetFEM MPI
documentation says:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Model RHS vectors are \sphinxstylestrong{globally assembled and replicated} on
every rank. A complete vector is expected and by itself is \sphinxstylestrong{not}
a reason to divide its values by P.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Tangent matrices are normally \sphinxstylestrong{distributed contributions};
the GetFEM\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}PETSc bridge must ADD these across ranks.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The original maintainer’s GetFEM 5.4.2 build instead returned
full replicated tangent matrices and P\sphinxhyphen{}fold nonlinear RHS terms;
this is a measured local behavior, \sphinxstylestrong{not} an assumption for 5.5.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
We explicitly audit native matrices, generic nonlinear RHS,
prescribed source RHS and their sum, separately, without invoking
SCRIMP’s normalization, PETSc transfer or MUMPS:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
mkdir\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}p\PYG{+w}{ }sandbox/outputs/getfem\PYGZhy{}assembly
\PYG{k}{for}\PYG{+w}{ }n\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{do}
\PYG{+w}{    }mpiexec\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}n}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }python\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}u\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{        }sandbox/diagnose\PYGZus{}getfem\PYGZus{}mpi\PYGZus{}assembly.py\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{        }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}output\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{sandbox/outputs/getfem\PYGZhy{}assembly/}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{n}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{.json}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{k}{done}

python\PYG{+w}{ }sandbox/analyze\PYGZus{}getfem\PYGZus{}mpi\PYGZus{}assembly.py\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }sandbox/outputs/getfem\PYGZhy{}assembly/*.json
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The analytical references on {[}0,1{]}, with u=1 and source=2,
are \sphinxhyphen{}1 for the generic RHS, +2 for the source\sphinxhyphen{}only RHS,
+1 for the mixed RHS, and 1/2 for the linear/nonlinear
tangent actions on a vector of ones.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The analyzer reports whether the generic RHS or source RHS
are \sphinxstylestrong{physical} or \sphinxstylestrong{P\sphinxhyphen{}fold duplicated}, and whether tangent
matrices are \sphinxstylestrong{full and replicated} or \sphinxstylestrong{distributed by
contribution}. The GetFEM 5.5 Docker build was measured with
correct raw generic and source RHS and distributed matrix
contributions on P=2/4. The Docker image therefore sets:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nv}{SCRIMP\PYGZus{}GETFEM\PYGZus{}MATRIX\PYGZus{}MODE}\PYG{o}{=}distributed
\PYG{n+nv}{SCRIMP\PYGZus{}GETFEM\PYGZus{}RHS\PYGZus{}MODE}\PYG{o}{=}auto
\PYG{n+nv}{SCRIMP\PYGZus{}GETFEM\PYGZus{}SOURCE\PYGZus{}RHS\PYGZus{}MODE}\PYG{o}{=}raw
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The default for non\sphinxhyphen{}Docker environments remains
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SCRIMP\_GETFEM\_MATRIX\_MODE=replicated}}, preserving the behavior
of the previously validated \sphinxstyleemphasis{local} GetFEM 5.4.2 installation.
For a freshly compiled GetFEM \sphinxstylestrong{never} copy these flags blindly:
first measure the native assembly with the diagnostic above, then
run its analyzer with the matching \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}matrix\sphinxhyphen{}mode replicated}}
or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}matrix\sphinxhyphen{}mode distributed}} parameter. For this GetFEM 5.5
container the mandatory CI command is:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
python\PYG{+w}{ }sandbox/analyze\PYGZus{}getfem\PYGZus{}mpi\PYGZus{}assembly.py\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}matrix\PYGZhy{}mode\PYG{+w}{ }distributed\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}require\PYGZhy{}physical\PYGZhy{}rhs\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }sandbox/outputs/getfem\PYGZhy{}assembly/*.json
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The RHS bridge calibrates generic contributions in
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SCRIMP\_GETFEM\_RHS\_MODE=auto}}, while
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SCRIMP\_GETFEM\_SOURCE\_RHS\_MODE=raw}}
preserves unscaled GetFEM source terms that are assembled once.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Do not change RHS normalization solely because GetFEM returns
full vectors or matrices.} First compare raw numerical values with
the known integrals and the P=1 reference. Preserve logs from
both GetFEM 5.4.2 and GetFEM 5.5 to distinguish an installation
issue from an upstream GetFEM convention.

\sphinxAtStartPar
GetFEM parallelism reference:
\sphinxhref{https://getfem.org/userdoc/parallel.html}{GetFEM parallel documentation}.


\subsection{2D wave Hamiltonian and boundary\sphinxhyphen{}power balance (MPI)}
\label{\detokenize{install:d-wave-hamiltonian-and-boundary-power-balance-mpi}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Before timing the parallel solver, validate the \sphinxstylestrong{undamped} wave
example’s port\sphinxhyphen{}Hamiltonian power identity using the same GetFEM
Hamiltonian integrands as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/wave.py}}. The prescribed
left\sphinxhyphen{}boundary input in the published example is nearly zero during
short smoke runs; a separate \sphinxstylestrong{nonzero boundary drive} prevents
vacuous energy\sphinxhyphen{}balance checks without changing the wave equations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the quadratic Hamiltonian and Crank\textendash{}Nicolson, check the discrete
midpoint identity (all four control ports have
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dissipative=True}}, meaning a positive \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{flow*effort}} is
subtracted from energy in SCRIMP’s existing plot convention):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}H(z_{k})-H(z_{k-1}) + (t_k-t_{k-1})
\sum_{\Gamma} \int_{\Gamma}
f_{\Gamma}(z_{k-1/2}) e_{\Gamma}(z_{k-1/2}) \,d\Gamma = 0.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The residual is calculated \sphinxstylestrong{per time step} at midpoint \sphinxstyleemphasis{state and
time}, not inferred from Hamiltonian conservation with zero input.
It also checks each scalar GetFEM integral is the same on every
rank before accepting it. The full Hamiltonian, each boundary
power trace, the signed work and the numerical defect are exported.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Inside the validated GetFEM 5.5 container (from repository root):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
mkdir\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}p\PYG{+w}{ }sandbox/outputs/energy
\PYG{k}{for}\PYG{+w}{ }n\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{do}
\PYG{+w}{    }mpiexec\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}oversubscribe\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}n}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{        }python\PYG{+w}{ }sandbox/check\PYGZus{}acoustic\PYGZus{}energy\PYGZus{}mpi.py\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{        }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}mesh\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}.2\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}dt\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}.002\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}final\PYGZhy{}time\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}.02\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{        }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}drive\PYGZhy{}left\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}0.08*sin(20*t)\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{        }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}output\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{sandbox/outputs/energy/wave\PYGZus{}}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{n}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{.json}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{k}{done}

python\PYG{+w}{ }sandbox/analyze\PYGZus{}acoustic\PYGZus{}power\PYGZus{}balance.py\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }sandbox/outputs/energy/wave\PYGZus{}*.json
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}diagnose\sphinxhyphen{}only}} to archive \sphinxstylestrong{raw measurements}, without
asserting an energy tolerance, when investigating a previously
unvalidated GetFEM build; do not describe such a run as validated.
CI uses a strict numeric gate and compares the complete Hamiltonian
and boundary\sphinxhyphen{}power trajectories at MPI 1, 2 and 4. Hosted CI uses
oversubscribed cores and its timing data are \sphinxstylestrong{not} suitable for
strong\sphinxhyphen{}scaling claims.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This check covers the \sphinxstyleemphasis{linear undamped acoustic problem}. It does
not yet prove energy consistency for nonlinear Saint\sphinxhyphen{}Venant models
or for substituted/dissipative ports.


\subsection{Optional SCRIMP phase profiling (without rebuilding GetFEM)}
\label{\detokenize{install:optional-scrimp-phase-profiling-without-rebuilding-getfem}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For v1.3.0 development, SCRIMP can measure its own GetFEM assembly
steps, GetFEM\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}PETSc transfers, DAE consistency initialization,
PETSc TS calls and implicit residual/Jacobian callbacks \sphinxstylestrong{per MPI rank}.
Profiling is disabled by default. It adds no MPI collectives inside
PETSc callbacks; reports are gathered explicitly after the solve.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Update the Python sources from the branch under development, then
reuse the \sphinxstylestrong{existing local Docker image} with a bind mount; no new
GetFEM compilation is necessary:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }pull\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}ff\PYGZhy{}only
mkdir\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}p\PYG{+w}{ }sandbox/outputs/scaling\PYGZhy{}profile
sudo\PYG{+w}{ }docker\PYG{+w}{ }run\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}rm\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}cpuset\PYGZhy{}cpus\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}0,2,4,6\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYGZhy{}e\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{SCRIMP\PYGZus{}MUMPS\PYGZus{}RESET\PYGZus{}PC\PYGZus{}ON\PYGZus{}JACOBIAN}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYGZhy{}v\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}PWD}\PYG{l+s+s2}{:/workspace/scrimp}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }scrimp\PYGZhy{}mpi:local\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }mpiexec\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}map\PYGZhy{}by\PYG{+w}{ }hwthread\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}bind\PYGZhy{}to\PYG{+w}{ }hwthread\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }python\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}u\PYG{+w}{ }sandbox/bench\PYGZus{}acoustic\PYGZus{}2d.py\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}mesh\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}.08\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}dt\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}.002\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}final\PYGZhy{}time\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}.04\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}save\PYGZhy{}dt\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}.01\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}profile\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}output\PYG{+w}{ }/workspace/scrimp/sandbox/outputs/scaling\PYGZhy{}profile/wave\PYGZus{}4.json
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The container’s non\sphinxhyphen{}root user needs write access to the chosen output
directory. Alternatively, write JSON under \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/tmp}} inside the
container and pipe/copy it to a local file. Without \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}profile}},
the original benchmark behaves as before.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In other DPHS scripts, set \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SCRIMP\_PROFILE=1}} \sphinxstylestrong{before} constructing
the DPHS and call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{system.get\_profile()}} on \sphinxstylestrong{every} MPI rank
after \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{system.solve()}}. The return value is JSON\sphinxhyphen{}serializable.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Reported wall durations use per\sphinxhyphen{}event MPI rank min/mean/max, and
record the number of calls. \sphinxstylestrong{Nested timers overlap}:
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{main.petsc.ts\_solve}} includes time spent in Python IFunction
and IJacobian callbacks, whose timings in turn include GetFEM and
PETSc bridge work. The derived \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{main.petsc.non\_callback\_remainder}}
subtracts callback durations on each rank; it includes factorization,
solve, monitoring and MPI waiting, and is \sphinxstylestrong{not pure MUMPS time}.
For the acoustic benchmark, add \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}petsc\sphinxhyphen{}log}} on a \sphinxstylestrong{separate
profiling run} to activate PETSc’s native event logger programmatically
(\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PETSc.Log.begin()}} before setup and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PETSc.Log.view()}} after
the simulation, collectively on all ranks). This distinction matters:
DPHS currently clears PETSc’s options database at construction,
so relying on the command\sphinxhyphen{}line \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}log\_view}} alone can be misleading.
PETSc’s printed summary contains native matrix, factorization and
solve events, including \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MatLUFactorSym}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MatLUFactorNum}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MatSolve}} when exposed by the linked PETSc build.

\sphinxAtStartPar
With \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SCRIMP\_MUMPS\_RESET\_PC\_ON\_JACOBIAN=1}}, the profiler also
reports \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{main.petsc.pc\_reset}} (inclusive in
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{main.petsc.callback.ijacobian}}). Do not disable this stability
workaround simply to improve benchmark timings without verifying
sparsity lifecycle and physical parity.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These measurements do not alter matrices, RHS scaling, equations
or the Crank\textendash{}Nicolson scheme.


\subsection{2D acoustic\sphinxhyphen{}wave strong scaling}
\label{\detokenize{install:d-acoustic-wave-strong-scaling}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The non\sphinxhyphen{}graphical \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sandbox/bench\_acoustic\_2d.py}} builds the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{existing} \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/wave.py}} model without modifying its
physical variational forms. It replaces only the spatial mesh
spacing, final integration horizon, numerical solver and output
frequency. It reports separately model construction/meshing,
complete solve (assembly + DAE initialization + PETSc TS),
peak rank RSS and physical state norms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstylestrong{strong scaling}, hold \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}mesh}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}dt}}
and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}final\sphinxhyphen{}time}} strictly fixed:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
mkdir\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}p\PYG{+w}{ }sandbox/outputs/scaling

\PYG{k}{for}\PYG{+w}{ }n\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{do}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n+nv}{SCRIMP\PYGZus{}MUMPS\PYGZus{}RESET\PYGZus{}PC\PYGZus{}ON\PYGZus{}JACOBIAN}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n+nv}{SCRIMP\PYGZus{}GETFEM\PYGZus{}SOURCE\PYGZus{}RHS\PYGZus{}MODE}\PYG{o}{=}raw\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }mpiexec\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}n}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }python\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}u\PYG{+w}{ }sandbox/bench\PYGZus{}acoustic\PYGZus{}2d.py\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{        }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}mesh\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}.05\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}dt\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}.001\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}final\PYGZhy{}time\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}.02\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{        }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}save\PYGZhy{}dt\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}.01\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{        }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}output\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{sandbox/outputs/scaling/wave\PYGZus{}}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{n}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ranks.json}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{        }\PYGZgt{}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{sandbox/outputs/scaling/wave\PYGZus{}}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{n}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ranks.log}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYGZgt{}\PYG{p}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{l+m}{1}
\PYG{k}{done}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To summarize multiple comparable runs automatically:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
python\PYG{+w}{ }sandbox/analyze\PYGZus{}acoustic\PYGZus{}scaling.py\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }sandbox/outputs/scaling/wave\PYGZus{}*ranks.json
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For more robust measurements, repeat each configuration several
times and provide all of the resulting JSON files to the analyzer.
It refuses mismatched meshes, end times, integrator settings or
significantly different physical field norms. The benchmark itself
exposes per\sphinxhyphen{}rank peak memory usage; for detailed PETSc timing,
append \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}log\_view}} to the command line and capture its log.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Report strong\sphinxhyphen{}scaling speedup
\(S_P=T_1/T_P\) and efficiency \(E_P=S_P/P\)
only for the \sphinxstylestrong{same mesh, time scheme, time horizon and
solver configuration}. Check final field norms and
all MPI convergence statuses first. Repeat runs and report
medians and variation: a single wall\sphinxhyphen{}clock number is not
a meaningful scaling study. Use PETSc \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}log\_view}} to
profile internal operations and separate GetFEM assembly,
MUMPS factorization, python\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}PETSc data transfer,
mesh construction and per\sphinxhyphen{}step all\sphinxhyphen{}rank gathers.


\subsection{Tests}
\label{\detokenize{install:tests}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Run targeted non\sphinxhyphen{}graphical tests with:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
python\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}m\PYG{+w}{ }unittest\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}v\PYG{+w}{ }tests.test\PYGZus{}lumped\PYGZus{}ports
mpiexec\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }python\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}m\PYG{+w}{ }unittest\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}v\PYG{+w}{ }tests.test\PYGZus{}mpi\PYGZus{}algebra
mpiexec\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }python\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}m\PYG{+w}{ }unittest\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}v\PYG{+w}{ }tests.test\PYGZus{}mpi\PYGZus{}algebra
mpiexec\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }python\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}m\PYG{+w}{ }unittest\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}v\PYG{+w}{ }tests.test\PYGZus{}mpi\PYGZus{}algebra
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The graphical examples below require a Matplotlib GUI backend:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
python\PYG{+w}{ }examples/mass\PYGZus{}spring\PYGZus{}damper.py
python\PYG{+w}{ }examples/nonlinear\PYGZus{}pendulum.py
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Code structure}
\label{\detokenize{install:code-structure}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{SCRIMP} is a Python package. The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scrimp/\_\_init\_\_.py}} file
is its root. For instance, the linear\sphinxhyphen{}algebra utilities can be
imported as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{import scrimp.utils.linalg}}.

\section{First SCRIMP project with VS Code (v1.3.0)}
\label{\detokenize{vscode:first-scrimp-project-with-vs-code-v1-3-0}}\label{\detokenize{vscode::doc}}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{important}{Important:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{public Linux/AMD64 image} \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ghcr.io/g\sphinxhyphen{}haine/scrimp:1.3.0}}
and stable Git tag \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{v1.3.0}} are published. The image passed
independent Ubuntu 24.04/AMD64 acceptance for the standalone
project, MPI startup and native Heat\textendash{}Wave Hamiltonian parity.
Windows/macOS, ARM64 and graphical multi\sphinxhyphen{}process MPI debugging
remain unqualified.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{What is on the user’s computer?}
\label{\detokenize{vscode:what-is-on-the-user-s-computer}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Docker with a precompiled image is the default v1.3.0 installation
path.} The native Conda route remains available for existing
users and advanced development. The user project ZIP is a
separate \sphinxhref{https://github.com/g-haine/scrimp/releases/tag/v1.3.0}{GitHub Release asset}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
After installation the user has \sphinxstylestrong{three separate components}:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Local VS Code (Python and, for Docker, Dev Containers extensions).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The SCRIMP numerical environment (a Docker image containing SCRIMP,
PETSc, SLEPc, GetFEM, Gmsh and Python; or a native Conda environment).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
An \sphinxstylestrong{independent local project} holding their simulations, geometry
inputs and persistent output files.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The project is independent from SCRIMP’s source repository. It works
with both a precompiled and locally built Docker image; the same
directory also works with a native Conda installation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The supplied project template creates this structure:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
MySCRIMPProject/
  .devcontainer/devcontainer.json
  .vscode/launch.json
  .vscode/tasks.json
  .vscode/settings.json
  simulations/first\PYGZus{}simulation.py
  simulations/mpi\PYGZus{}check.py
  geometries/
  outputs/
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first example is a genuine serial port\sphinxhyphen{}Hamiltonian
mass\sphinxhyphen{}spring\sphinxhyphen{}damper simulation and saves outputs/oscillator.csv.
The second script checks MPI startup, \sphinxstylestrong{not physical MPI parity}.


\subsection{Creating the independent workspace}
\label{\detokenize{vscode:creating-the-independent-workspace}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Download \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scrimp\sphinxhyphen{}project\sphinxhyphen{}template.zip}} from the
\sphinxhref{https://github.com/g-haine/scrimp/releases/tag/v1.3.0}{v1.3.0 GitHub Release}
and extract it as your own project. The official archive
already selects \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ghcr.io/g\sphinxhyphen{}haine/scrimp:1.3.0}} in the
Dev Container configuration.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Maintainers can rebuild the user ZIP with:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
python3\PYG{+w}{ }scripts/package\PYGZhy{}scrimp\PYGZhy{}project\PYGZhy{}template.py\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}image\PYG{+w}{ }ghcr.io/g\PYGZhy{}haine/scrimp:1.3.0
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This produces an archive only; it does not publish an image.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For source customization (not required with the release ZIP):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nv}{BOOTSTRAP}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{k}{\PYGZdl{}(}mktemp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}d\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}t\PYG{+w}{ }scrimp\PYGZhy{}starter.XXXXXXXX\PYG{k}{)}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}
git\PYG{+w}{ }clone\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}depth\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}branch\PYG{+w}{ }v1.3.0\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }https://github.com/g\PYGZhy{}haine/scrimp.git\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}BOOTSTRAP}\PYG{l+s+s2}{/source}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}
python3\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}BOOTSTRAP}\PYG{l+s+s2}{/source/scripts/create\PYGZhy{}scrimp\PYGZhy{}project.py}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}HOME}\PYG{l+s+s2}{/MySCRIMPProject}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}image\PYG{+w}{ }ghcr.io/g\PYGZhy{}haine/scrimp:1.3.0
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The BOOTSTRAP directory is a separate \sphinxstylestrong{newly created} temporary
source checkout. The user’s new project is in MySCRIMPProject and
can be retained indefinitely. The temporary source checkout can
be removed after successful project creation; never remove an
existing user directory to make room for it.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The generator refuses to overwrite any pre\sphinxhyphen{}existing directory and
never copies the source repository’s sandbox, output data or Git history.
To package the user project from source:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
python3\PYG{+w}{ }scripts/package\PYGZhy{}scrimp\PYGZhy{}project\PYGZhy{}template.py\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}image\PYG{+w}{ }ghcr.io/g\PYGZhy{}haine/scrimp:1.3.0
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{A. Precompiled Docker installation (recommended)}
\label{\detokenize{vscode:a-precompiled-docker-installation-recommended}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pull the qualified, public Linux/AMD64 image:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
docker\PYG{+w}{ }pull\PYG{+w}{ }ghcr.io/g\PYGZhy{}haine/scrimp:1.3.0
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
No compilation or SCRIMP source checkout is required. The image is
stored in Docker’s image store, \sphinxstyleemphasis{not} in the user’s simulations folder.
The official release ZIP selects the stable image by default.
For a project generated from a historical source\sphinxhyphen{}tree
template, explicitly use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}image ghcr.io/g\sphinxhyphen{}haine/scrimp:1.3.0}}.


\subsection{B. Locally compiled Docker installation}
\label{\detokenize{vscode:b-locally-compiled-docker-installation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A developer can rebuild the same candidate from a specific GitHub
revision. The official build driver fetches that revision into a
temporary checkout and stages only tracked, allowlisted source files
into an isolated Docker context:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} In a temporary checkout of SCRIMP:}
bash\PYG{+w}{ }scripts/build\PYGZhy{}v130\PYGZhy{}docker\PYGZhy{}candidate.sh
bash\PYG{+w}{ }scripts/smoke\PYGZhy{}v130\PYGZhy{}docker\PYGZhy{}candidate.sh
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Dev Containers image selection (Linux validation finding):}
Use an \sphinxstylestrong{explicit complete image reference} in
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.devcontainer/devcontainer.json}}, including its tag:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nt}{\PYGZdq{}image\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}scrimp\PYGZhy{}mpi:v1.3.0\PYGZhy{}rc1\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the first VS Code GUI attempt, the template’s expression
\sphinxtitleref{\$\{localEnv:SCRIMP\_DOCKER\_IMAGE:scrimp\sphinxhyphen{}mpi:v1.3.0\sphinxhyphen{}rc1\}}
was incorrectly resolved to just \sphinxtitleref{scrimp\sphinxhyphen{}mpi}. VS Code
then attempted to fetch \sphinxtitleref{scrimp\sphinxhyphen{}mpi:latest} from Docker Hub and
failed. This was \sphinxstylestrong{not} a Docker permissions or SCRIMP runtime
failure. The starter now uses the literal candidate tag. For a
different built image, edit the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{image}} property or generate
the project with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}image IMAGE:TAG}}. Projects created before
the fix must update their \sphinxstylestrong{own copy} of devcontainer.json;
pulling the SCRIMP Git repository does not modify existing
independent projects.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The initial \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scrimp\sphinxhyphen{}mpi:v1.3.0\sphinxhyphen{}rc1}} image \sphinxstylestrong{passed its
first native Docker build and 1/2\sphinxhyphen{}rank CLI smoke on
19 November 2026}, including a scaffolded project and an
actual serial oscillator simulation. That is \sphinxstyleemphasis{historical}
qualification. The final \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dist\sphinxhyphen{}rc4}} image passed fresh\sphinxhyphen{}host GetFEM/PETSc/MUMPS
and MPI acceptance; it was promoted \sphinxstylestrong{unchanged} to public
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ghcr.io/g\sphinxhyphen{}haine/scrimp:1.3.0}}. Historic source templates may
still reference a local \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rc1}} candidate; select the stable tag. The Docker build \sphinxstylestrong{does
not access any local simulations}, even from a developer checkout.
Explicit library development with uncommitted changes uses
SCRIMP\_DOCKER\_SOURCE=local (still using physical source staging).
A user only modifying simulations never rebuilds the image.


\subsection{VS Code workflow for either Docker installation}
\label{\detokenize{vscode:vs-code-workflow-for-either-docker-installation}}\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Install Docker and VS Code with Python and Dev Containers extensions.
On Windows use Docker Desktop with WSL2; on macOS use Docker Desktop.
Both paths are \sphinxstylestrong{best effort for existing users} and are not
independent native Windows/macOS acceptance tests for v1.3.0.
See {\hyperref[\detokenize{install::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{How to install}}}} for executable shell commands, WSL2 volume
guidance and the Apple Silicon image\sphinxhyphen{}architecture/emulation caveat.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Open \sphinxstylestrong{MySCRIMPProject} in VS Code (not SCRIMP’s source checkout).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Choose \sphinxstylestrong{Dev Containers: Reopen in Container}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check the selected interpreter is
/opt/conda/envs/scrimp/bin/python.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Run the following in the VS Code integrated terminal:

\end{enumerate}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
python\PYG{+w}{ }simulations/first\PYGZus{}simulation.py
mpiexec\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }python\PYG{+w}{ }simulations/mpi\PYGZus{}check.py
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Python is installed, even if VS Code says “No Python found”}
\label{\detokenize{vscode:python-is-installed-even-if-vs-code-says-no-python-found}}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{important}{Important:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Do not click “Install uv and Python”} when opening a SCRIMP
Dev Container. The image \sphinxstylestrong{already contains Python}, installed
in the named Micromamba environment \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scrimp}} along with
SCRIMP, GetFEM, PETSc and SLEPc. Installing another Python with
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{uv}} would create an unrelated interpreter and might leave
VS Code running code outside the qualified numerical environment.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
During the first Linux Dev Containers GUI test (19 November 2026),
VS Code displayed:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
No Python found. Would you like to install uv and use it to
install Python?
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This message comes from \sphinxstylestrong{VS Code’s Python environment discovery /
installation UI}, not from SCRIMP or the Python runtime. The
subsequent integrated terminal showed \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{(scrimp)}}, and both
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{python simulations/first\_simulation.py}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpiexec \sphinxhyphen{}n 2 python simulations/mpi\_check.py}} \sphinxstylestrong{passed}.
Therefore that specific prompt was a \sphinxstylestrong{false negative for the
already installed container interpreter}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{When this prompt appears:}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Select \sphinxstylestrong{Don’t ask again} (or \sphinxstylestrong{Cancel} to dismiss without
installing anything). Do not select \sphinxstylestrong{Install uv and Python}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Wait until the Dev Container has fully opened and the Python
extension has completed initialization.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Open a Python file, press \sphinxstylestrong{Ctrl+Shift+P}, select
\sphinxstylestrong{Python: Select Interpreter}, then choose \sphinxstylestrong{Enter interpreter
path} and enter \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/opt/conda/envs/scrimp/bin/python}} if
that interpreter is not already selected. Depending on VS Code’s
extension version, the command/labels may differ slightly.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Confirm the environment in the \sphinxstylestrong{Dev Container’s integrated
terminal}, not in a host terminal:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
python\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}c\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}import sys, scrimp; print(sys.executable); print(\PYGZsq{}SCRIMP OK\PYGZsq{})\PYGZdq{}}
python\PYG{+w}{ }simulations/first\PYGZus{}simulation.py
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Expected first line of the interpreter check:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{opt}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{conda}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{envs}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{scrimp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n+nb}{bin}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{python}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the terminal test passes but \sphinxstylestrong{F5} still cannot find Python,
check that the Microsoft \sphinxstylestrong{Python} and \sphinxstylestrong{Python Debugger}
extensions are installed \sphinxstylestrong{in Dev Container: SCRIMP}, not
only in the local VS Code window. Restart the Python extension /
reload the VS Code window, and explicitly select the interpreter
above. This is an editor integration problem, not an indication
that the numerical image needs rebuilding.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The starter’s \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.devcontainer/devcontainer.json}} already declares
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{python.defaultInterpreterPath}} as the Conda interpreter
\sphinxstylestrong{inside the container}. VS Code’s environment\sphinxhyphen{}discovery UI may
still present a generic first\sphinxhyphen{}run message before selection
completes. The native Conda installation path uses the
\sphinxstylestrong{actual local} interpreter instead; do not force the container
path into \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.vscode/settings.json}} shared by both modes.


\subsection{Python environment recognition and editable SCRIMP imports}
\label{\detokenize{vscode:python-environment-recognition-and-editable-scrimp-imports}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Ubuntu Dev Containers tests revealed two \sphinxstylestrong{distinct} editor
integration problems, even though SCRIMP executed and debugged:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pylance initially reported \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Import "scrimp" could not be
resolved}}. The image uses \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pip install \sphinxhyphen{}e .}}, with the
editable sources located in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/workspace/scrimp/scrimp/}}.
Adding \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{python.analysis.extraPaths=/workspace/scrimp}}
resolved the warning \sphinxstylestrong{in the actual VS Code GUI}. This does
not suppress diagnostics for genuinely missing packages.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The separate \sphinxtitleref{Python Environments} extension repeatedly
proposed installing Python and later declared the selected
interpreter invalid. \sphinxstylestrong{After clearing and reselecting the
interpreter, the error persisted.} The Python extension
logged both \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Active interpreter {[}/work{]}:
/opt/conda/envs/scrimp/bin/python}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{No Python environment is set for this resource}}.
The executable is correct and already installed, but the
environment manager fails to associate it with the workspace.
SCRIMP uses Micromamba rather than a standard Conda executable.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Confirmed correction on Ubuntu (20 Nov 2026):} opt out of the
new Python Environments integration \sphinxstylestrong{in this Dev Container only},
while retaining Microsoft’s Python extension, Pylance and debugpy.
When the user added the missing
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{"python.useEnvironmentsExtension": false}} setting to their
\sphinxstyleemphasis{existing local project} they reported that the interpreter
warning disappeared. Pylance’s missing\sphinxhyphen{}import warning had
already been eliminated independently by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{extraPaths}}.
The Python extension documents its supported legacy setting
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{python.useEnvironmentsExtension=false}}. Similar invalid
interpreter reports have been filed against Python Environments.
The project template’s \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.devcontainer/devcontainer.json}}
now uses these \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{customizations.vscode.settings}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nt}{\PYGZdq{}python.defaultInterpreterPath\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}/opt/conda/envs/scrimp/bin/python\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nt}{\PYGZdq{}python.useEnvironmentsExtension\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kc}{false}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nt}{\PYGZdq{}python.interpreter.infoVisibility\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}always\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nt}{\PYGZdq{}python.analysis.extraPaths\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}/workspace/scrimp\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{],}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nt}{\PYGZdq{}python.terminal.activateEnvironment\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kc}{false}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
There is \sphinxstylestrong{no need for} \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{python\sphinxhyphen{}envs.globalSearchPaths}}
when the new manager is disabled. The legacy Python extension
should instead use the explicitly selected interpreter.
Python itself and the SCRIMP image are unchanged; this setting
does not uninstall any extension.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Update an existing project} (Git pull does not update its
independent files):
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Open \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textless{}project\textgreater{}/.devcontainer/devcontainer.json}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Under \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{customizations.vscode.settings}}, add
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{"python.useEnvironmentsExtension": false}}
and remove \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{"python\sphinxhyphen{}envs.globalSearchPaths"}}.
Keep the absolute \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{python.defaultInterpreterPath}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{python.analysis.extraPaths}} and the complete Docker
image tag intact.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Select \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Developer: Reload Window}} in VS Code. If
Dev Containers does not apply the remote settings, select
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Dev Containers: Rebuild and Reopen in Container}}.
This reuses the local image; it does \sphinxstylestrong{not} recompile any
numerical dependencies or copy the user’s simulations.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Open a Python file and check whether the invalid\sphinxhyphen{}interpreter
notification is gone. If necessary, use
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Python: Clear Workspace Interpreter Setting}}, then
select \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/opt/conda/envs/scrimp/bin/python}} with
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Python: Select Interpreter}}. The already validated
F5 debugger and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{import scrimp}} should remain functional.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Observed Ubuntu Dev Containers acceptance: PASS.} After the
setting was added to the user’s existing project, VS Code stopped
reporting the invalid interpreter. The serial simulation, 2\sphinxhyphen{}rank
MPI startup and F5/debugpy run had already passed. The template
contains the same settings for future projects. This is not
yet a clean\sphinxhyphen{}room test on a new machine or a cross\sphinxhyphen{}platform
compatibility claim. If a future extension update reintroduces
the prompt, inspect the Python extension logs; do not install
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{uv}}, suppress real Pylance errors or modify the numerical
image to work around an editor\sphinxhyphen{}only problem.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All container\sphinxhyphen{}only absolute paths remain in Dev Container
metadata, \sphinxstylestrong{not} the shared \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.vscode/settings.json}}: native
Conda installations select their own local interpreters.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The host project is bind\sphinxhyphen{}mounted at /work. The first command
writes MySCRIMPProject/outputs/oscillator.csv \sphinxstylestrong{on the host}.
Closing VS Code or removing the container does not delete that file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The included VS Code Run and Debug configurations support \sphinxstylestrong{F5}
for a serial simulation or the active Python file; MPI multiprocess
debugging requires a separate setup. VS Code Tasks also provide
the first simulation and a two\sphinxhyphen{}rank MPI smoke.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Verified on Ubuntu Dev Containers (20 November 2026):} the user
opened \sphinxtitleref{simulations/first\_simulation.py}, started the

The terminal showed execution via

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a first debugging session:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Open \sphinxtitleref{simulations/first\_simulation.py} in VS Code.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Click in the gutter beside \sphinxtitleref{system = S.DPHS(“real”)}
to add a \sphinxstylestrong{red breakpoint}.

\item {}

Press \sphinxstylestrong{F5} and select \sphinxstylestrong{SCRIMP: first simulation}.

\item {}

When paused (yellow current\sphinxhyphen{}line arrow), press \sphinxstylestrong{F10}

\item {}

Press \sphinxstylestrong{F5} to resume execution, or \sphinxstylestrong{Shift+F5} to

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is a \sphinxstylestrong{serial Python debugging} validation. Debugging
simultaneous MPI worker ranks, and breakpoints inside compiled
GetFEM/PETSc/MUMPS C/C++/Fortran code, are different workflows
and are \sphinxstylestrong{not} qualified by this Python test.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Modern SCRIMP examples create \sphinxstylestrong{one} output tree per working
directory: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{outputs/\textless{}system\_name\textgreater{}/\{png,svg,gif,mesh,log,npz,json\}}}.
Importing SCRIMP does \sphinxstylestrong{not} pre\sphinxhyphen{}create generic
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{outputs/log}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{outputs/mesh}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{outputs/png}}
or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{outputs/pv}} siblings. Historical unscoped \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Domain}}
and explicitly configured legacy output callers retain
their old paths; existing archived user files are not deleted.
Linux Dev Containers attempts to map the mambauser UID/GID to that
of the host user. Test host output\sphinxhyphen{}directory permissions before
large runs; Windows and macOS use different Docker Desktop volume
semantics.

\sphinxAtStartPar
CPU/NUMA selection should be recorded for performance benchmarks.
Do not use MPI \textendash{}oversubscribe as evidence of strong scaling: it is
appropriate only for small functional tests when the host has too
few CPUs.


\subsection{Using an existing local sandbox directory}
\label{\detokenize{vscode:using-an-existing-local-sandbox-directory}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Developers may already have many personal simulations under their
SCRIMP source checkout’s sandbox/. \sphinxstylestrong{They do not need to move or copy
those files.} The Linux command\sphinxhyphen{}line runner binds the existing
sandbox directory at /work at runtime:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZti{}/Simulations/scrimp
\PYG{n+nv}{SCRIMP\PYGZus{}SIM\PYGZus{}DIR}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}PWD}\PYG{l+s+s2}{/sandbox}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }bash\PYG{+w}{ }scripts/run\PYGZhy{}v130\PYGZhy{}docker\PYGZhy{}simulation.sh\PYG{+w}{ }wave\PYGZus{}1D.py
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This command is \sphinxstylestrong{not an image build}. The Python script is read from
the local sandbox; its results stay under sandbox/outputs/. Change the
script name to run another local simulation, or set SCRIMP\_MPI\_RANKS=2
for a script that is actually MPI\sphinxhyphen{}compatible. The runner is currently
a Linux/macOS shell development convenience, \sphinxstylestrong{not} the final
cross\sphinxhyphen{}platform user installer. It still requires a successfully
built/pulled SCRIMP Docker image.

\label{\detokenize{vscode:c-native-conda-source-installation-without-docker}}

Use the native build instructions in {\hyperref[\detokenize{install::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{How to install}}}} for the intended
platform. Then activate the installed Conda environment:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
conda\PYG{+w}{ }activate\PYG{+w}{ }scrimp55\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} for the native modern\PYGZhy{}stack example in install.rst}

mpiexec\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }python\PYG{+w}{ }simulations/mpi\PYGZus{}check.py
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Open this \sphinxstylestrong{same project} in VS Code, select \sphinxstylestrong{Python: Select
Interpreter} and choose the Conda interpreter. Do not select
Reopen in Container. Native installation is distinct from compiling
