\subsection{Maxwell equations in 3D — patched Nédélec\sphinxhyphen{}II / BDM1 example}
\label{\detokenize{examples/maxwell_3d:maxwell-equations-in-3d-patched-nedelec-ii-bdm1-example}}\label{\detokenize{examples/maxwell_3d::doc}}

\subsubsection{Why a new Maxwell example?}
\label{\detokenize{examples/maxwell_3d:why-a-new-maxwell-example}}\label{\detokenize{examples/maxwell_3d:maxwell-3d}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The wave tutorials {\hyperref[\detokenize{examples/wave::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{The wave equation — 2A: conservative anisotropic membrane}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{examples/wave_coenergy::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{The wave equation — 2C: co\sphinxhyphen{}energy and localized damping}}}} work
in two spatial dimensions. This is an intentionally \sphinxstylestrong{tiny
genuine 3D test}: a homogeneous sphere, just two vector
unknowns, no sources, no feedback controllers, and four
weak\sphinxhyphen{}form bricks. It exercises the corrected \sphinxstylestrong{intrinsic
vector finite elements} in the pinned SCRIMP GetFEM 5.5
image, not ordinary componentwise CG vector elements.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This example is \sphinxstylestrong{new}, independent of the published
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{COMPEL\_2025/Maxwell\_2D.py}} research script (which is
not modified), and of the 2D Nédélec\sphinxhyphen{}independent
wave benchmark.


\subsubsection{A normalized Maxwell system}
\label{\detokenize{examples/maxwell_3d:a-normalized-maxwell-system}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(\Omega\) be the unit ball in
\(\mathbb R^3\), filled with a homogeneous,
isotropic, lossless material with \sphinxstylestrong{dimensionless}
\(\varepsilon=\mu=1\). The electric field
\(E\) and the magnetic induction \(B\) satisfy
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\partial_t E = \operatorname{curl} B,\qquad
\partial_t B = -\operatorname{curl} E,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
without free currents or sources. Initially,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E(0,x,y,z)=(-y,x,0),\qquad B(0)=0.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The electric field has nonzero curl and
zero divergence initially. It is an exact
low\sphinxhyphen{}order edge\sphinxhyphen{}element\sphinxhyphen{}type polynomial and
excites a nontrivial magnetic field.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The true 3D domain and both co\sphinxhyphen{}energy/state
declarations come directly from the executable:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{model}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{set\PYGZus{}domain}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{S}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Domain}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Ball}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{R}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{l+m+mf}{1.}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{h}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{n+nb}{float}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{mesh\PYGZus{}size}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{k}{if} \PYG{n}{model}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{domain}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}dim}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{o}{!=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{3}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{k}{raise} \PYG{n+ne}{RuntimeError}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Maxwell requires a genuine 3D volume mesh}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{E} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{S}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{State}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{E}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Electric field}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{vector\PYGZhy{}field}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{B} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{S}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{State}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{B}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Magnetic induction}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{vector\PYGZhy{}field}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{model}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}state}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{E}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{model}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}state}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{B}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{model}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}costate}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{S}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{CoState}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{e\PYGZus{}E}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Electric field}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{E}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{substituted}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{True}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{model}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}costate}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{S}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{CoState}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{e\PYGZus{}B}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Magnetic induction}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{B}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{substituted}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{True}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}

\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The coupling uses the \sphinxstylestrong{homogeneous natural
boundary closure} of the weak form, namely
zero magnetic tangential boundary work, not an
explicitly imposed electric PEC trace and not
a driven port. The discrete model closes the
boundary power balance by construction. This
small demonstration does not claim strong
boundary\sphinxhyphen{}trace or electromagnetic eigenmode
accuracy.


\subsubsection{Compatible 3D spaces and their GetFEM patches}
\label{\detokenize{examples/maxwell_3d:compatible-3d-spaces-and-their-getfem-patches}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
We use the \sphinxstylestrong{SCRIMP\sphinxhyphen{}patched} pair on genuine tetrahedra:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E_h \in \mathrm{N\acute ed\acute elec}_{\mathrm{II},1}
     \subset H(\mathrm{curl};\Omega),\qquad
B_h \in \mathrm{BDM}_1
     \subset H(\mathrm{div};\Omega).\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
On each tetrahedron, both fields have local polynomial
shape functions in \([P_1]^3\); the Nédélec\sphinxhyphen{}II
edge DOFs impose tangential continuity, while BDM1
face DOFs impose normal continuity. In particular
\(\operatorname{curl} E_h\) is piecewise
constant and belongs to the divergence\sphinxhyphen{}free
subspace of BDM1, compatible with Maxwell’s
magnetic Gauss law.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Important distinction:} the original accepted
baseline at source commit \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{daac18cb}} used
GetFEM’s \sphinxstyleemphasis{built\sphinxhyphen{}in} lowest Nédélec
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FEM\_NEDELEC(3)}} with built\sphinxhyphen{}in RT0. It
did \sphinxstylestrong{not} exercise SCRIMP’s new element patches.
The current tutorial now explicitly uses
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FEM\_NEDELEC2(3,1)}} (patch \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{0004}}) and
tetrahedral \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FEM\_BDMK(3,1)}} (patch \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{0001}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
These FE names use the new SCRIMP shortcuts
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{S.FEM("E", 1, "NED2")}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{S.FEM("B", 1, "BDM")}}. Additional
shortcuts \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NED1}} / \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NEDELEC1}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NED2}} / \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NEDELEC2}} are mapped by
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scrimp/fem.py}} to the corresponding
GetFEM constructors. The number in
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NED1}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NED2}} is the \sphinxstylestrong{family
(1st/2nd kind)}, while the numeric argument
is the \sphinxstylestrong{polynomial order k}. Patch 0004
supports only k=1 or 2.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Nedelec0/RT0. NED2 k=1 \PYGZhy{}\PYGZgt{} FEM\PYGZus{}NEDELEC2(3,1) (patch 0004),}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} BDM k=1 \PYGZhy{}\PYGZgt{} FEM\PYGZus{}BDMK(3,1) (tetrahedral DoF patch 0001).}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} curl([P1]\PYGZca{}3) is constant and is contained in BDM1;}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} exact div(curl(E)) = 0 is preserved by the mass equation.}
\PYG{n}{fem\PYGZus{}E} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{S}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{FEM}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{E}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{NED2}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{fem\PYGZus{}B} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{S}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{FEM}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{B}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{BDM}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} S.FEM has a legacy silent CG fallback on native AssertionError.}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Retain these exact objects to detect it after registration.}
\PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{fem}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{expected\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{expected\PYGZus{}order} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{p}{(}
    \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{fem\PYGZus{}E}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{NED2}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{fem\PYGZus{}B}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{BDM}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{n}{model}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}FEM}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{fem}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{n}{assert\PYGZus{}patched\PYGZus{}intrinsic\PYGZus{}fem}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{fem}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{expected\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{expected\PYGZus{}order}\PYG{p}{)}

\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A strict post\sphinxhyphen{}registration guard retains both
original \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{S.FEM}} objects and verifies that
their \sphinxstylestrong{type and order are unchanged} after
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{DPHS.add\_FEM()}}, and that the actual GetFEM
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MeshFem}} has vector dimension 3 and
nonzero degrees of freedom. This is important:
SCRIMP’s existing FEM adapter \sphinxstyleemphasis{mutates the
original type/order to CG/1} on GetFEM’s
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{AssertionError}} fallback. A silent
replacement is thus explicitly detected,
without relying on the Python binding’s
version\sphinxhyphen{}dependent \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MeshFem.fem()}} layout.
This runtime guard is \sphinxstylestrong{not yet a complete
proof of Maxwell numerical correctness}.


\subsubsection{A skew\sphinxhyphen{}adjoint discrete Maxwell interconnection}
\label{\detokenize{examples/maxwell_3d:a-skew-adjoint-discrete-maxwell-interconnection}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The weak formulation is deliberately minimal:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}(\partial_t E_h,v_h)_{L^2(\Omega)}
   &= (B_h,\operatorname{curl}v_h)_{L^2(\Omega)},\\
(\partial_t B_h,w_h)_{L^2(\Omega)}
   &= -(\operatorname{curl}E_h,w_h)_{L^2(\Omega)}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The GetFEM generic weak\sphinxhyphen{}form language does
not supply a portable built\sphinxhyphen{}in 3D \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Curl}} in
this image. The canonical example defines
the operator explicitly from the 3x3 gradient
tensor, \sphinxstylestrong{without} imposing an ad hoc
stencil or swapping the curl orientation:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{CURL3} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{(}
    \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{[Grad(v)(3,2)\PYGZhy{}Grad(v)(2,3);}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}
    \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Grad(v)(1,3)\PYGZhy{}Grad(v)(3,1);}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}
    \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Grad(v)(2,1)\PYGZhy{}Grad(v)(1,2)]}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{p}{)}




\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are only \sphinxstylestrong{four} variational bricks:
two mass blocks and the two mutually
opposite curl couplings. They are
skew\sphinxhyphen{}adjoint in the discrete GetFEM
mass inner products.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{brick} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{p}{(}
    \PYG{n}{S}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Brick}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{M\PYGZus{}E}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{E.Test\PYGZus{}E}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{dt}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{True}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{position}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{flow}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{S}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Brick}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{M\PYGZus{}B}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{B.Test\PYGZus{}B}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{dt}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{True}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{position}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{flow}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{S}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Brick}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{C\PYGZca{}T}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{B.Curl3(Test\PYGZus{}E)}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{position}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{effort}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{S}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Brick}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZhy{}C}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZhy{}Curl3(E).Test\PYGZus{}B}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{position}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{effort}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{n}{model}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}brick}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{brick}\PYG{p}{)}

\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The original electromagnetic Hamiltonian is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathcal H(t) = \frac12\int_{\Omega}
   (|E_h|^2+|B_h|^2)\,\mathrm dx.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The semidiscrete identity follows by
testing the first equation with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{E\_h}}
and the second with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{B\_h}}:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{\mathrm d\mathcal H}{\mathrm dt}
=(B_h,\operatorname{curl}E_h)
 -(\operatorname{curl}E_h,B_h)=0.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The initial data and CN integration
are explicitly defined in the runnable
source, including the absence of any
unnecessary algebraic DAE projection:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} zero magnetic field; curl E=[0,0,2] triggers nontrivial dynamics.}
\PYG{n}{model}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{set\PYGZus{}initial\PYGZus{}value}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{E}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{[\PYGZhy{}y, x, 0.]}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{model}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{set\PYGZus{}initial\PYGZus{}value}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{B}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{[0., 0., 0.]}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{n}{model}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{set\PYGZus{}time\PYGZus{}scheme}\PYG{p}{(}
    \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Both states carry a positive mass: this is an ODE, NOT a DAE.}
    \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} The algebraic initializer requires algebraic unknowns;}
    \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} a pseudo\PYGZhy{}TS or artificial DAE spin\PYGZhy{}up would be wrong here.}
    \PYG{n}{init\PYGZus{}step}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{False}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{ts\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{cn}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{ts\PYGZus{}adapt\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{none}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{ts\PYGZus{}exact\PYGZus{}final\PYGZus{}time}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{matchstep}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{t\PYGZus{}0}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{t\PYGZus{}f}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n+nb}{float}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{final\PYGZus{}time}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{dt}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n+nb}{float}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{time\PYGZus{}step}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{dt\PYGZus{}save}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n+nb}{float}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{time\PYGZus{}step}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{ksp\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{gmres}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{pc\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{lu}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{pc\PYGZus{}factor\PYGZus{}mat\PYGZus{}solver\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{factor\PYGZus{}solver}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{model}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{solve}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}

\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The original two positive electromagnetic
energy terms are likewise the canonical
GetFEM Hamiltonian, not recomputed from
an invented displacement field:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{model}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{hamiltonian}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{set\PYGZus{}name}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{3D electromagnetic energy}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{model}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{hamiltonian}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}term}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{S}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Term}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Electric}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{0.5*E.E}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{model}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{hamiltonian}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}term}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{S}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Term}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Magnetic}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{0.5*B.B}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{k}{return} \PYG{n}{model}


\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{fixed Crank\textendash{}Nicolson} scheme has
the corresponding \sphinxstyleemphasis{exact quadratic}
discrete identity:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathcal H^{n+1}-\mathcal H^n
 =\Delta t\left[
   (B_h^{n+1/2},\operatorname{curl}E_h^{n+1/2})
  -(\operatorname{curl}E_h^{n+1/2},B_h^{n+1/2})
  \right]=0.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Both variables are differential, so
there is \sphinxstylestrong{no algebraic DAE initial
projection} or pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}time spin\sphinxhyphen{}up.
Initial data are projected into their
exact native finite\sphinxhyphen{}element spaces.


\subsubsection{How to run and qualify this 3D example}
\label{\detokenize{examples/maxwell_3d:how-to-run-and-qualify-this-3d-example}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
We separate a \sphinxstylestrong{source contract} from
real native numerical acceptance.
The qualification runner uses the same
pinned GetFEM/PETSc/MUMPS Docker image
as the 2D examples. It checks
10 fixed CN steps at \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{h=0.7}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dt=0.02}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{t\_f=0.2}},
on \sphinxstylestrong{MPI 1 and MPI 2}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZti{}/Simulations/scrimp
git\PYG{+w}{ }pull\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}ff\PYGZhy{}only
conda\PYG{+w}{ }activate\PYG{+w}{ }scrimp

\PYG{n+nv}{SCRIMP\PYGZus{}DOCKER\PYGZus{}NO\PYGZus{}SUDO}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{n+nv}{SCRIMP\PYGZus{}V130\PYGZus{}DAE\PYGZus{}IMAGE}\PYG{o}{=}scrimp\PYGZhy{}mpi:v1.3.0\PYGZhy{}rc3\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
bash\PYG{+w}{ }scripts/run\PYGZhy{}v130\PYGZhy{}maxwell3d\PYGZhy{}pilot.sh
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The runner will only print
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PASS\_MAXWELL3D\_MUMPS\_MPI1\_MPI2}} if all
native checks succeed. It saves even
failed traces to
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sandbox/outputs/v130\sphinxhyphen{}maxwell3d\sphinxhyphen{}*.zip}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{physical gates} include the
presence of a genuine 3D mesh,
real patched Nédélec\sphinxhyphen{}II/BDM1 spaces, exact ten\sphinxhyphen{}step
fixed CN integration, positive initial
electromagnetic energy, nontrivial magnetic
excitation, and agreement between GetFEM
Hamiltonian values and independent
electric/magnetic volume quadratures.
Every\sphinxhyphen{}step and cumulative energy defects
must be below \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{1e\sphinxhyphen{}9}} times the
physical energy scale. All MPI rank traces
and MPI1/MPI2 results are compared.
The divergence of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{B}} is independently
measured by GetFEM’s squared L2 norm
and \sphinxstylestrong{checked} against the compatible
discrete Gauss law. Its initial value is
zero and, for the compatible Nédélec\sphinxhyphen{}II k1
and BDM1 spaces, the discrete curl maps into
the divergence\sphinxhyphen{}free BDM subspace. This is an
actual additional acceptance gate,
\sphinxstylestrong{not} a claim of convergence of all
Maxwell constraints. The electric Gauss
law and electromagnetic boundary\sphinxhyphen{}mode
accuracy are outside this minimal pilot.

\sphinxAtStartPar
After a native PASS, the archive contains
true complete FE histories (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rank*.npz}}),
original energy/diagnostic values, JSON
acceptance metadata, and two \sphinxstylestrong{genuine
3D ParaView PVD time series} for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{E}}
and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{B}} (11 VTU snapshots each).
Open \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mumps\_mpi1/pv/E/E.pvd}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mumps\_mpi1/pv/B/B.pvd}} in ParaView;
view the 3D vectors with a cut plane,
glyphs, or streamlines.

\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{H\_B(0.2)=0.25824828616211315}}
for MPI1. The total electromagnetic
Hamiltonian is conserved with a maximum
defect \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{4.11e\sphinxhyphen{}15}}, while about
\sphinxstylestrong{37.20\%} of the initial electric energy
is stored magnetically at \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{t=0.2}}.
The independent GetFEM magnetic\sphinxhyphen{}divergence
integral \(\int_{\Omega}(\operatorname{div} B)^2\,\mathrm dx\) remains
at most \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{4.2153e\sphinxhyphen{}28}} on MPI1.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The maximum coefficient difference between
full MPI1 and MPI2 FE histories
(11 times, 1,269 unknowns) is
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{2.1094237467877974e\sphinxhyphen{}15}}.
Each MPI2 rank saved an identical
trajectory, with its SHA256 verified.
\sphinxstylestrong{All five graphics} are generated from
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{same run} by
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/maxwell\_3d.py \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}export}},

GIF}. The integrated renderer is
therefore \sphinxstylestrong{qualified in MPI1 and MPI2},
not just source\sphinxhyphen{}tested. The true vector
VTU exports and original time samples

The earlier source commit \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{daac18cb}}
was a valid \sphinxstylestrong{separate baseline} using
GetFEM native Nédélec0/RT0 (497 DOFs),
not a test of either patched family.
Neither the new or the old qualification
establishes mesh/time convergence,
electric Gauss\sphinxhyphen{}law validity, explicit PEC
boundary conditions, cavity eigenmodes,
or SuperLU\_DIST acceptance.

of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{(div B)\textasciicircum{}2}}, with

\subsection{Mass\textendash{}spring\textendash{}damper}
\label{\detokenize{examples/mass_spring_damper:mass-spring-damper}}\label{\detokenize{examples/mass_spring_damper::doc}}

\subsubsection{A two\sphinxhyphen{}state finite\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional port\sphinxhyphen{}Hamiltonian model}
\label{\detokenize{examples/mass_spring_damper:a-two-state-finite-dimensional-port-hamiltonian-model}}\label{\detokenize{examples/mass_spring_damper:id1}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(q\) be the displacement of a point mass, \(p=m\dot q\)
its momentum, \(m>0\) the mass, \(k>0\) the stiffness and
\(c\geq0\) the viscous damping coefficient. The applied force
is \(f(t)\). Then
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\dot q = \frac{p}{m},\qquad
\dot p = -kq-\frac{c}{m}p+f(t).\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the energy variables \(z=(q,p)^\top\) and Hamiltonian
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}H(z)=\frac12 kq^2+\frac{p^2}{2m}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The co\sphinxhyphen{}energy variables are
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}e_q=\frac{\partial H}{\partial q}=kq,\qquad
e_p=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p}=\frac{p}{m}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The port\sphinxhyphen{}Hamiltonian representation is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\dot z =
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}}_{J}
\begin{bmatrix}e_q\\e_p\end{bmatrix}
-\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&c\end{bmatrix}}_{R}
\begin{bmatrix}e_q\\e_p\end{bmatrix}
+\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}f(t),\qquad
y=e_p.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Since \(J=-J^\top\) and \(R\succeq0\), the continuous
power balance is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\dot H=-c\,e_p^2+f(t)e_p.\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Discretization and code}
\label{\detokenize{examples/mass_spring_damper:discretization-and-code}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This is an ODE, not a spatial PDE. The new \sphinxtitleref{lumped} port kind
assigns \sphinxstylestrong{one} GetFEM DOF to each state and its co\sphinxhyphen{}state.
The reference interval \((0,1)\) in the script is only used
to assemble scalar GetFEM weak forms; it is not a physical spring mesh.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The implementation follows the standard SCRIMP workflow:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Create a \sphinxtitleref{DPHS} and its reference \sphinxtitleref{Domain}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Add two \sphinxtitleref{State} objects with \sphinxtitleref{kind=”lumped”}, and their \sphinxtitleref{CoState} objects.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Call \sphinxtitleref{add\_lumped\_port} for \sphinxtitleref{q} and \sphinxtitleref{p} (not \sphinxtitleref{add\_FEM}).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Add mass, interconnection, damping, forcing and constitutive \sphinxtitleref{Brick} objects.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Initialize the two states \sphinxstylestrong{and their constitutive co\sphinxhyphen{}energies},
integrate with implicit PETSc BDF2, then plot.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The factor \sphinxtitleref{/ell} in each brick compensates for the integration over
the reference interval length \sphinxtitleref{ell}, so that the resulting scalar
equations are exactly those above. The time\sphinxhyphen{}dependent forcing is
assembled as a nonlinear/residual brick rather than as a fixed matrix
term; this is needed in SCRIMP’s current GetFEM assembly path.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Initial consistency is not a time\sphinxhyphen{}integration step.} The dynamical
initial values are prescribed as \sphinxtitleref{q0=0.4}, \sphinxtitleref{p0=0}. Since this
finite\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional model has explicit constitutive laws, the exact
algebraic initialization is simply
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}e_q(0)=kq_0=2,\qquad e_p(0)=p_0/m=0.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The example now assigns these two genuine scalar GetFEM co\sphinxhyphen{}energy
variables directly and disables pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}time relaxation. This preserves
\sphinxstylestrong{all} physical initial data instead of moving the momentum to
satisfy the constraints. It does not change the mass, interconnection,
damping, forcing or the subsequent BDF2 integrator. The generic SCRIMP
DAE initializers are unchanged.

\subsubsection{Verification}
\label{\detokenize{examples/mass_spring_damper:verification}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The expected energy variation satisfies
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}H(t)-H(0)=\int_0^t\bigl[f(s)e_p(s)-c\,e_p(s)^2\bigr],\mathrm ds.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The continuous work integral is useful for understanding the physics,
but it should \sphinxstylestrong{not} be confused with the \sphinxstylestrong{generic
nodal\sphinxhyphen{}trapezoid plot}, which is only an approximation
for BDF2 ({\hyperref[\detokenize{energy_and_power::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Energy, powers and time discretization (v1.3.0)}}}}). This
specific example separately measures its own discrete
quadratic identity, not an identity supplied by
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{compute\_powers()}}. This example uses the original quadratic Hamiltonian and
fixed\sphinxhyphen{}step BDF2, so every step \(n\geq2\) also has the exact
\sphinxstyleemphasis{discrete} quadratic identity
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{
    H(z_n)-H(z_{n-1})
    +H(2z_n-z_{n-1})-H(2z_{n-1}-z_{n-2})
    +H(z_n-2z_{n-1}+z_{n-2})
}{2\Delta t}
+c\left(\frac{p_n}{m}\right)^2
-f(t_n)\frac{p_n}{m}=0.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This identity is obtained by multiplying the \sphinxstylestrong{original}
semi\sphinxhyphen{}discrete oscillator equation by its current co\sphinxhyphen{}energy, not
by applying a trapezoidal rule to a saved power plot.
It covers BDF2 steps \(n\geq2\), not the internal PETSc
\sphinxstylestrong{BDF2 startup stages}, which require a separate analysis.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The native qualification checks the physical model, BDF2 time
stepping and GetFEM weak forms, starting from exactly consistent
algebraic co\sphinxhyphen{}energies with no artificial initial time step.
It uses MUMPS in MPI 1 and 2 and measures the actual algebraic
relations
\(e_q=kq\), \(e_p=p/m\), both differentiated BDF2
equations, the exact step energy\sphinxhyphen{}power defect and the complete
MPI state trajectory. The independent reference is the
\sphinxstylestrong{forced two\sphinxhyphen{}state ODE}, integrated by a high\sphinxhyphen{}accuracy RK4
scheme, not a replacement SCRIMP model:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{g+go}{SCRIMP\PYGZus{}DOCKER\PYGZus{}NO\PYGZus{}SUDO=1 \PYGZbs{}\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{g+go}{SCRIMP\PYGZus{}V130\PYGZus{}DAE\PYGZus{}IMAGE=scrimp\PYGZhy{}mpi:v1.3.0\PYGZhy{}rc3 \PYGZbs{}\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{g+go}{bash scripts/run\PYGZhy{}v130\PYGZhy{}mass\PYGZhy{}spring\PYGZhy{}physical\PYGZhy{}pilot.sh}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The exact\sphinxhyphen{}initialization short pilot has PASSED}
its native GetFEM/PETSc MPI1/MPI2 scientific checks:
\sphinxtitleref{q\_0=.4,p\_0=0,e\_\{q,0\}=2,e\_\{p,0\}=0} exactly,
maximum exact BDF2 step energy\sphinxhyphen{}power defect
\sphinxtitleref{4.21e\sphinxhyphen{}14}, maximum complete DAE MPI1/2 discrepancy
\sphinxtitleref{3.47e\sphinxhyphen{}18}, and an independent RK4 forced\sphinxhyphen{}ODE error
\sphinxtitleref{6.00e\sphinxhyphen{}5} over the eight physical steps.

\subsection{Nonlinear pendulum}
\label{\detokenize{examples/nonlinear_pendulum:nonlinear-pendulum}}\label{\detokenize{examples/nonlinear_pendulum::doc}}

\subsubsection{A nonlinear port\sphinxhyphen{}Hamiltonian ODE}
\label{\detokenize{examples/nonlinear_pendulum:a-nonlinear-port-hamiltonian-ode}}\label{\detokenize{examples/nonlinear_pendulum:id1}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Consider a point mass \(m\) on a massless rod of length
\(\ell\), rotating in a vertical plane under gravity \(g\).
Let \(\theta\) denote its angle, \(I=m\ell^2\) the
moment of inertia and \(p=I\dot\theta\) its angular momentum.
An optional external torque \(\tau(t)\) and viscous damping
\(d\geq0\) complete the model:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\dot\theta = \frac{p}{I},\qquad
\dot p=-mg\ell\sin\theta-\frac{d}{I}p+\tau(t).\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The energy is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}H(\theta,p)=\frac{p^2}{2I}
              +mg\ell(1-\cos\theta).\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
It follows that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}e_\theta=mg\ell\sin\theta,\qquad
e_p=\frac{p}{I}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The canonical port\sphinxhyphen{}Hamiltonian representation uses
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{bmatrix}\dot\theta\\\dot p\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}e_\theta\\e_p\end{bmatrix}
-
\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&d\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}e_\theta\\e_p\end{bmatrix}
+
\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}\tau(t).\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The power balance reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\dot H=-d\,e_p^2+\tau(t)e_p.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This example intentionally uses the full
\(\sin\theta\) relation, \sphinxstylestrong{not} the small\sphinxhyphen{}angle approximation.


\subsubsection{Implementation notes}
\label{\detokenize{examples/nonlinear_pendulum:implementation-notes}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The states \sphinxtitleref{theta} and \sphinxtitleref{p} and their corresponding efforts are
global \sphinxtitleref{lumped} variables with one degree of freedom each. The
nonlinear constitutive law is written with an explicitly nonlinear
GetFEM brick:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{S}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Brick}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{CR\PYGZus{}theta\PYGZus{}nonlinear}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
        \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{gravity\PYGZus{}torque*sin(theta)*Test\PYGZus{}e\PYGZus{}theta/ell}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
        \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{linear}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{False}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The GetFEM reference interval is only a weak\sphinxhyphen{}form assembly support,
and the \sphinxtitleref{/ell} normalization yields a single ODE residual.
All variables are spatially constant.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The example now initializes its \sphinxstylestrong{exact constitutive co\sphinxhyphen{}energies}
from the original nonlinear sine law, preserving the prescribed
initial differential data, without a pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}time evolution:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\theta_0=1.2,\qquad p_0=0,\qquad
e_{\theta,0}=mg\ell\sin(1.2),\qquad e_{p,0}=0.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The full sine GetFEM weak formulation, constitutive bricks,
damping and forcing are retained. The canonical example uses
\sphinxstylestrong{one} physical time scheme: PETSc \sphinxtitleref{ts\_type=”cn”}, fixed time step,
without any pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}time initialization. The former BDF2 short
qualification was a useful diagnostic but \sphinxstylestrong{does not qualify CN}.
The exact\sphinxhyphen{}initial\sphinxhyphen{}state CN formulation has now passed
the short and complete twelve\sphinxhyphen{}second native scientific
qualification described below.

\subsubsection{Numerical validation — Crank\textendash{}Nicolson}
\label{\detokenize{examples/nonlinear_pendulum:numerical-validation-cranknicolson}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The canonical example now uses \sphinxstylestrong{PETSc Crank\textendash{}Nicolson} only.
In PETSc 3.26, \sphinxtitleref{ts\_type=”cn”} means the \sphinxstylestrong{endpoint trapezoidal}
method, not the implicit midpoint method. Define the endpoint
average \(\bar a_n=(a_{n-1}+a_n)/2\). At every step,
the expected equations are
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
\frac{\theta_n-\theta_{n-1}}{\Delta t}
   &= \bar e_{p,n},\\
\frac{p_n-p_{n-1}}{\Delta t}
   &= -\bar e_{\theta,n}-d\,\bar e_{p,n}
      +\bar\tau_n.
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The corresponding \sphinxstylestrong{exact discrete co\sphinxhyphen{}energy power pairing}
tests the actual CN residual:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\bar e_{\theta,n}
   \frac{\theta_n-\theta_{n-1}}{\Delta t}
+\bar e_{p,n}
   \frac{p_n-p_{n-1}}{\Delta t}
+d\,\bar e_{p,n}^2
-\bar\tau_n\,\bar e_{p,n}=0.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
However, \(H=p^2/(2I)+mg\ell(1-\cos\theta)\)
is nonquadratic. The endpoint\sphinxhyphen{}averaged nonlinear effort
is \sphinxstylestrong{not an exact discrete gradient}. Consequently,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{H_n-H_{n-1}}{\Delta t}
=\bar\tau_n\,\bar e_{p,n}
 -d\,\bar e_{p,n}^{2}
 +\Gamma_n,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\Gamma_n\) is the \sphinxstylestrong{measured CN nonlinear
chain\sphinxhyphen{}rule defect}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Gamma_n=
   \frac{H_n-H_{n-1}
   -\bar e_{\theta,n}(\theta_n-\theta_{n-1})
   -\bar e_{p,n}(p_n-p_{n-1})}{\Delta t}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The canonical \sphinxtitleref{python examples/nonlinear\_pendulum.py} directly
saves native trajectory, phase portrait, nonlinear energy/power
plots (PNG/SVG) and a \sphinxstylestrong{schematic} GIF, all from actually
accepted GetFEM states. Files are written to
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{outputs/nonlinear\_pendulum\_free/}},
with images under \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{png/}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{svg/}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gif/}},
and original numerical histories under \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{npz/}}.
The forced variant, called with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{torque\_amplitude=0.1}},
writes instead to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{outputs/nonlinear\_pendulum\_forced/}}.
Both also save the generic \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{plot\_Hamiltonian()}}
PNG/SVG/NPZ outputs.
The plots explicitly distinguish true changes of \(H\),
CN discrete port work and dissipation, and the chain\sphinxhyphen{}rule
defect; no exact Hamiltonian conservation is implied.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The original CN short physical pilot has \sphinxstylestrong{PASSED natively}:
eight accepted steps (\sphinxtitleref{dt=.01}, \sphinxtitleref{t\_f=.08}), both
unforced and forced torque cases, MUMPS MPI1 and MPI2.
All four lumped GetFEM DAE variables agreed to
\sphinxtitleref{1.11e\sphinxhyphen{}16} across MPI configurations. The maximum
nonlinear CN co\sphinxhyphen{}energy power defect was \sphinxtitleref{1.43e\sphinxhyphen{}13},
the nonlinear Hamiltonian chain\sphinxhyphen{}rule accounting closed
to \sphinxtitleref{3.35e\sphinxhyphen{}15}, and the maximum deviation from an
independent full\sphinxhyphen{}sine RK4 solution was \sphinxtitleref{2.27e\sphinxhyphen{}5}.
The genuine native archive and SHA256 checksum are
recorded in \sphinxtitleref{docs/V130\_NONLINEAR\_PENDULUM\_PHYSICAL\_ACCEPTANCE.md}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The full \sphinxstylestrong{twelve\sphinxhyphen{}second} canonical CN acceptance
also \sphinxstylestrong{PASSED natively} on 26 November 2026. It
includes \sphinxstylestrong{1200 steps} in MPI1/MPI2, a \sphinxstylestrong{2400\sphinxhyphen{}step
refinement} in MPI1, and the original
program\sphinxhyphen{}generated PNG/SVG/GIF for both free and
forced motion. The verified run is reproducible using:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{g+go}{SCRIMP\PYGZus{}DOCKER\PYGZus{}NO\PYGZus{}SUDO=1 \PYGZbs{}\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{g+go}{SCRIMP\PYGZus{}V130\PYGZus{}DAE\PYGZus{}IMAGE=scrimp\PYGZhy{}mpi:v1.3.0\PYGZhy{}rc3 \PYGZbs{}\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{g+go}{bash scripts/run\PYGZhy{}v130\PYGZhy{}nonlinear\PYGZhy{}pendulum\PYGZhy{}CN\PYGZhy{}full\PYGZhy{}showcase.sh}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The full test independently recomputes the true original
GetFEM \sphinxtitleref{sin(theta)} constitutive law, Hamiltonian,
endpoint CN equation/power residuals and the nonlinear
chain\sphinxhyphen{}rule correction from all \sphinxstylestrong{1201 accepted four\sphinxhyphen{}DOF
GetFEM snapshots} in both MPI1 and MPI2. Complete
MPI1/MPI2 state differences are bounded by
\sphinxtitleref{1.02e\sphinxhyphen{}13}. Against an independent full\sphinxhyphen{}sine RK4
reference, the maximum trajectory errors on the
coarse and refined time grids decrease with ratios
\sphinxtitleref{3.999772} (free) and \sphinxtitleref{3.999606} (forced),
giving observed orders \sphinxstylestrong{1.999918} and \sphinxstylestrong{1.999858}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The example itself generated and saved, for both
physics variants, the verified trajectory, phase
portrait and energy/power PNG/SVG graphics and the
36\sphinxhyphen{}frame schematic motion GIF. Its saved state
histories were compared directly to the original
native GetFEM records. The 74\sphinxhyphen{}member evidence ZIP
\sphinxtitleref{v130\sphinxhyphen{}pendulum\sphinxhyphen{}CN\sphinxhyphen{}12s\sphinxhyphen{}showcase\sphinxhyphen{}b93cfd27\sphinxhyphen{}Kd1WLVcv.zip}
passed CRC and independent numerical inspection.
For the exact source commit, Docker image and
archive SHA256, see
\sphinxtitleref{docs/V130\_NONLINEAR\_PENDULUM\_PHYSICAL\_ACCEPTANCE.md}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}

MUMPS MPI1/MPI2 configurations, including temporal

The exact Hamiltonian conservation of a
nonquadratic system is \sphinxstylestrong{not} claimed: the

initialization}. The strict initializer maintains the prescribed
temperature field exactly and solves for the algebraic variables with
an accuracy target of \sphinxtitleref{1e\sphinxhyphen{}13}. This is a setting of this example,
\sphinxstylestrong{not} a global change to the SCRIMP initializer. The semi\sphinxhyphen{}discrete
GetFEM model, conductivity, mass, three temperature boundary controls
and the left mixed Neumann/feedback boundary are unchanged.

Run the real example directly; \sphinxstylestrong{no sandbox visualization script is
required}:

\end{sphinxVerbatim}

The example writes into \sphinxstylestrong{one system output root},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{outputs/heat/}} (not global \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{outputs/png}} or
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{outputs/showcase}}). It creates the real GetFEM

\subsubsection{Setting}
\label{\detokenize{examples/heat:setting}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This example is the first simple case of intrinsically port\sphinxhyphen{}Hamiltonian
Differential Algebraic Equation (known as pH\sphinxhyphen{}DAE).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The so\sphinxhyphen{}called \sphinxstyleemphasis{heat equation} is driven by the first law of
thermodynamics.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(\Omega = (0,2) \times (0,1)\) be a bounded open connected set,
with mass density \(\rho(x)\), for all \(x \in \Omega\), and
\(n\) be the outward unit normal at the boundary
\(\partial\Omega\). We assume that:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The domain \(\Omega\) does not change over time: \sphinxstyleemphasis{i.e.} we work
at constant volume in a solid

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
No chemical reaction is to be found in the domain

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dulong\sphinxhyphen{}Petit’s model: internal energy is proportional to temperature

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let us denotes:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(u\) the internal energy density

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\mathbf{J}_Q\) the heat flux

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(T\) the local temperature

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(C_V := \left( \frac{d u}{d T} \right)_V\) the isochoric heat
capacity

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first law of thermodynamics, stating that in an isolated system, the
energy is preserved, reads:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\rho(x) \partial_t u(t, x) = - {\rm div} \left( J_Q(t, x) \right), \qquad \forall t \ge 0, x \in \Omega.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Under Dulong\sphinxhyphen{}Petit’s model, one has \(u = C_V T\), which leads to
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\rho(x) C_V(x) \partial_t T(t, x) = - {\rm div} \left( J_Q(t, x) \right), \qquad \forall t \ge 0, x \in \Omega.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As constitutive relation, the classical Fourier’s law is considered:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}J_Q(t, x) = - \lambda(x) \cdot {\rm grad} \left( T(t, x) \right), \qquad \forall t \ge 0, x \in \Omega,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\lambda\) is the \sphinxstylestrong{tensor\sphinxhyphen{}valued} heat conductivity of the
medium.

\sphinxAtStartPar
We assume furthermore that one wants to control the temperature
\(T = u_D\) at the lower, right and upper part of the boundary,
denoted \(\Gamma_D\) (a \sphinxstylestrong{D}irichlet boundary condition), while
the inward heat flux \(-J_Q \cdot n = u_N\) will be prescribed at
the left edge, denoted \(\Gamma_N\) (a \sphinxstylestrong{N}eumann boundary
condition). Thus, the observations are \(y_D = - J_Q \cdot n\) and
\(y_N = T\) respectively.


\subsubsection{Port\sphinxhyphen{}Hamiltonian framework}
\label{\detokenize{examples/heat:port-hamiltonian-framework}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let us choose as Hamiltonian the usual quadratic form for parabolic
equation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathcal{H}(T(t,x)) := \frac{1}{2} \int_\Omega \rho(x) Cv(x) T^2(t,x) {\rm d}x.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Computing the variational derivative with respect to the weigthed
\(L^2\)\sphinxhyphen{}inner product
\(\left( \phi, \psi \right)_\Omega := \int_\Omega \rho(x) C_V(x) \phi(x) \psi(x) {\rm d} x\)
leads to a co\sphinxhyphen{}state variable \(e_T = T\). Hence, the first law of
thermodynamics may be written as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{pmatrix} \rho C_V T \\ \star \end{pmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -{\rm div} \\ \star & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} T \\ J_Q \end{pmatrix}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As we want a \sphinxstyleemphasis{formally} skew\sphinxhyphen{}symmetric \(J\) operator, it has to be
completed with \(-{\rm grad}\), then
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{pmatrix} \rho C_V T \\ f_Q \end{pmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -{\rm div} \\ -{\rm grad} & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} T \\ J_Q \end{pmatrix},\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and Fourier’s law provides the constitutive relation
\(J_Q = \lambda f_Q\) to close the system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Remark:} \(\rho C_V\) appears against the state variable as the
weight of the \(L^2\)\sphinxhyphen{}inner product, it should not be ommited in the
mass matrix at the discrete level.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{power balance} satisfied by the \sphinxstylestrong{Hamiltonian} is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{\rm d}{{\rm d}t} \mathcal{H}(t) = \underbrace{- \int_\Omega \lambda \| f_Q(t,x) \|^2 {\rm d} x}_{\text{dissipated power}} \underbrace{+ \left\langle u_D(t,\cdot), y_D(t,\cdot) \right\rangle_{\Gamma_D}}_{\text{power flowing through }\Gamma_D} \underbrace{+ \left\langle y_N(t,\cdot), u_N(t,\cdot)\right\rangle_{\Gamma_N}}_{\text{power flowing through }\Gamma_N},\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\left\langle \cdot, \cdot \right\rangle_{\Gamma}\) is a
boundary duality bracket \(H^\frac12, H^{-\frac12}\) at the boundary
\(\Gamma\).


\subsubsection{Structure\sphinxhyphen{}preserving discretization}
\label{\detokenize{examples/heat:structure-preserving-discretization}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(\varphi_T\) and \(\varphi_Q\) be smooth test functions on
\(\Omega\), and \(\psi_N\) and \(\psi_D\) be smooth test
functions on \(\Gamma_N\) and \(\Gamma_D\) respectively. One can
write the weak formulation of the \sphinxstylestrong{Dirac Structure} as follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\lbrace
\begin{array}{rcl}
\int_\Omega \rho(x) C_V(x) \partial_t T(t,x) \varphi_T(x) {\rm d}x &=& - \int_\Omega {\rm div} \left( J_Q(t,x) \right) \varphi_T(x) {\rm d}x, \\
\int_\Omega f_Q(t,x) \cdot \varphi_Q(x) {\rm d}x &=& - \int_\Omega {\rm grad} \left( T(t,x) \right) \cdot \varphi_Q(x) {\rm d}x, \\
\left\langle y_D, \psi_D \right\rangle_{\Gamma_D} &=& \left\langle -J_Q \cdot n, \psi_D \right\rangle_{\Gamma_D}, \\
\left\langle u_N, \psi_N \right\rangle_{\Gamma_N} &=& \left\langle -J_Q \cdot n, \psi_N \right\rangle_{\Gamma_N}.
\end{array}
\right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Integrating by parts the second line make the control \(u_N\) and
the observation \(y_D\) appear
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\int_\Omega f_Q(t,x) \cdot \varphi_Q(x) {\rm d}x = \int_\Omega T(t,x) {\rm div} \left( \varphi_Q(x) \right) {\rm d}x - \left\langle u_D, \varphi_Q \cdot n \right\rangle_{\Gamma_D} - \left\langle y_N, \varphi_Q \cdot n \right\rangle_{\Gamma_N}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar

\((\varphi_Q^k)_{1 \le k \le N_Q} \subset H_{\rm div}(\Omega)\) be
two finite families of approximations for the \(T\)\sphinxhyphen{}type port and
the \(Q\)\sphinxhyphen{}type port respectively, typically discontinuous and
continuous Galerkin finite elements respectively. Denote also
\((\psi_N^m)_{1 \le m_N \le N_N} \subset H^{\frac12}(\Gamma_N)\) and
\((\psi_D^m)_{1 \le m_N \le N_D} \subset H^{\frac12}(\Gamma_D)\). In
particular, the latter choices imply that the duality brackets at the
boundary reduce to simple \(L^2\) scalar products.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Writing the discrete weak formulation with those families, one has for

\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\lbrace
\begin{array}{rcl}
\sum_{j=1}^{N_T} \int_\Omega \varphi_T^j(x) \rho(x) C_V(x) \varphi_T^i(x) {\rm d}x \, \frac{\rm d}{{\rm d}t} T^j(t) &=& - \sum_{\ell=1}^{N_Q} \int_\Omega {\rm div} \left( \varphi_Q^\ell(x) \right) \varphi_T^i(x) {\rm d}x \, J_Q^\ell(t), \\
\sum_{\ell=1}^{N_Q} \int_\Omega \varphi_Q^\ell(x) \varphi_Q^k(x) {\rm d}x \, f_Q^\ell(t) &=& \sum_{j=1}^{N_Q} \int_\Omega \varphi_T^j(x) {\rm div} \left( \varphi_Q^k(x) \right) {\rm d}x \, T^j(t) \\
&& \quad - \sum_{n_D=1}^{N_D} \int_{\Gamma_D} \varphi_Q^k(s) \cdot n(s) \psi_D^{n_D}(s) {\rm d}s \, u_D^{n_D}(t) \\
&& \qquad - \sum_{n_N=1}^{N_N} \int_{\Gamma_N} \varphi_Q^k(s) \cdot n(s) \psi_N^{n_N}(s) {\rm d}s \, y_N^{n_N}(t), \\
\sum_{n_D=1}^{N_D} \left\langle \psi_D^{n_D}, \psi_D^{m_D} \right\rangle_{\Gamma_D} \, y_D^{n_D}(t) &=& - \sum_{\ell=1}^{N_p} \int_{\Gamma_D} \varphi_Q^\ell(s) \cdot n(s) \psi_D^{m_D}(s) {\rm d}s \, J_Q^\ell(t), \\
\sum_{n_N=1}^{N_N} \left\langle \psi_N^{n_N}, \psi_N^{m_N} \right\rangle_{\Gamma_N} \, u_N^{n_N}(t) &=& - \sum_{\ell=1}^{N_p} \int_{\Gamma_N} \varphi_Q^\ell(s) \cdot n(s) \psi_N^{m_N}(s) {\rm d}s \, J_Q^\ell(t),

0 & 0 & 0 & M_N

\begin{pmatrix}

\underline{J_Q}(t) \\

\begin{split}(M_D)_{m_Dn_D} := \int_{\Gamma_D} \psi_D^{n_D}(s) \psi_D^{m_D}(s) {\rm d}s,

\begin{split}(D)_{i\ell} := - \int_\Omega {\rm div} \left( \varphi_Q^\ell(x) \right) \cdot \varphi_T^i(x) {\rm d}x\end{split}

\begin{split}(B_D)_{n_Dk} := - \int_{\Gamma_D} \varphi_Q^k(s) \cdot n(s) \psi_D^{n_D}(s) {\rm d}s,

\sphinxAtStartPar
As controls, we assume that the temperature is prescribed, while the
inward heat flux is proportional to the temperature (\sphinxstyleemphasis{i.e.} we consider
an impedance\sphinxhyphen{}like absorbing boundary condition). This is easily achieved
in \sphinxstylestrong{SCRIMP} by calling the variable in the expression of the control
to apply.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The initial temperature profile is compatible with these controls, and
has a positive bump centered in the domain.

\PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{control\PYGZus{}port}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{expression} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n+nb}{zip}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{control\PYGZus{}ports}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{expressions}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Set the control functions (automatic construction of bricks such that \PYGZhy{}M\PYGZus{}u u + f(t) = 0)}
    \PYG{n}{heat}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{set\PYGZus{}control}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{control\PYGZus{}port}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}name}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{expression}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Set the initial data}
\PYG{n}{heat}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{set\PYGZus{}initial\PYGZus{}value}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{T}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{1. + 2.*np.exp(\PYGZhy{}50*((x\PYGZhy{}1)*(x\PYGZhy{}1)+(y\PYGZhy{}0.5)*(y\PYGZhy{}0.5))**2)}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
We can now solve our Differential Algebraic Equation (DAE) using,
\sphinxstyleemphasis{e.g.}, a Backward Differentiation Formula (BDF) of order 4.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{}\PYGZsh{} Solve in time}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Define the time scheme (\PYGZdq{}bdf\PYGZdq{} is backward differentiation formula)}
\PYG{n}{heat}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{set\PYGZus{}time\PYGZus{}scheme}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{t\PYGZus{}f}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mf}{5.}\PYG{p}{,}
                     \PYG{n}{ts\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{bdf}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
                     \PYG{n}{ts\PYGZus{}bdf\PYGZus{}order}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mi}{4}\PYG{p}{,}
                     \PYG{n}{dt}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.01}\PYG{p}{,}
                     \PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Solve}
\PYG{n}{heat}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{solve}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Hamiltonian may be defined, computed and plot.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{}\PYGZsh{} Post\PYGZhy{}processing}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Set Hamiltonian name}
\PYG{n}{heat}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{hamiltonian}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{set\PYGZus{}name}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Lyapunov formulation}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Define the term}
\PYG{n}{terms} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{[}
    \PYG{n}{S}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Term}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{L\PYGZca{}2\PYGZhy{}norm}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{0.5*T*rho*T}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{]}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Add them to the Hamiltonian}
\PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{term} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n}{terms}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{n}{heat}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{hamiltonian}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}term}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{term}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Plot the Hamiltonian}
\PYG{n}{heat}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{plot\PYGZus{}Hamiltonian}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{save\PYGZus{}figure}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{True}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{filename}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Hamiltonian\PYGZus{}Heat\PYGZus{}2D.png}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A physically oriented, energy\sphinxhyphen{}dissipative coupled heat\sphinxhyphen{}wave example.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Reference: Haine, Matignon \& Monteghetti, Mathematical Reports (2022),
eqs. (2.1)\sphinxhyphen{}(2.2), (3.15), (4.3)\sphinxhyphen{}(4.5). This example is NOT the paper’s
numerical experiment: it keeps the original SCRIMP heat div\sphinxhyphen{}div and
wave grad\sphinxhyphen{}grad weak forms, choosing compatible mixed FEM spaces.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The original built\sphinxhyphen{}in Concentric geometry has disk=1, annulus=2,
interface=10, outer boundary=20. CN and the 0\sphinxhyphen{}input external
Dirichlet condition are used to expose the heat dissipation and
closed interconnection in an interpretable power balance.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Interface normals always mean each subdomain’s outward normal.
The conservative two\sphinxhyphen{}sided conforming interface compiler is
enabled by default in the v1.3.0 release\sphinxhyphen{}preparation source.
Physical labels, FEM declarations and weak forms are unchanged.
Ambiguous or unsupported interfaces fail explicitly; use
SCRIMP\_AUTO\_INTERFACE=0 only to recover legacy manual assembly
if your model was already oriented by hand.

“constrained\_l2” computes the closest zero\sphinxhyphen{}trace field in the

\subsubsection{Run and inspect the canonical example}
\label{\detokenize{examples/heat_wave:run-and-inspect-the-canonical-example}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The updated v1.3.0 \sphinxstylestrong{source} now exposes the two heat/wave
subsystem energies and their interface transfer directly
in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{original} example. The following command produces
real original GetFEM/PETSc states (not synthetic figures).
The strict \sphinxstylestrong{full nine\sphinxhyphen{}case native example\sphinxhyphen{}output
campaign passed on 27 November 2026}, commit \sphinxtitleref{20d79d0d},
including Heat\textendash{}Wave MPI2 and a ZIP CRC check.
All cases use a single \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{outputs/\textless{}system\_name\textgreater{}/}} directory,
without legacy global output siblings. This acceptance
covers these original GetFEM/PETSc example configurations,
not arbitrary user\sphinxhyphen{}supplied PDE models.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
python\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}m\PYG{+w}{ }examples.heat\PYGZus{}wave\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}final\PYGZhy{}time\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}.2\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}time\PYGZhy{}step\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}.002\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}save\PYGZhy{}step\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}.002
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Files are stored in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{./outputs/heat\_wave/}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
outputs/heat\PYGZus{}wave/
  png/       Hamiltonian\PYGZus{}Heat1\PYGZus{}Wave2\PYGZus{}2D.png
             heat\PYGZus{}wave\PYGZus{}subsystem\PYGZus{}energies.png
             heat\PYGZus{}wave\PYGZus{}interface\PYGZus{}powers.png
             heat\PYGZus{}wave\PYGZus{}energy\PYGZus{}work.png
  svg/       (corresponding vector figures)
  mesh/      Concentric.msh, T/T.pvd, p/p.pvd
             (original GetFEM VTU time series)
  log/       scrimp.log
  npz/       heat\PYGZus{}wave\PYGZus{}observables.npz
  json/      heat\PYGZus{}wave\PYGZus{}observables.json
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The canonical \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{plot\_Hamiltonian}} method additionally
saves \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{npz/Hamiltonian\_Heat1\_Wave2\_2D.npz}} containing
the numerical original Hamiltonian terms and
explicitly classified port powers. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{p}} represents
the wave velocity, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{q}} its stress, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{T}}
the heat\sphinxhyphen{}side temperature.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The energy figure plots separately
\(H_H(t)\), \(H_W(t)\) and
\(H_H(t)+H_W(t)\). The powers figure
plots \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{U\_T*Y\_T}} on the heat side and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{U\_w*Y\_w}} on the wave side, \sphinxstylestrong{using two
distinct, outward\sphinxhyphen{}oriented interface facets}.
The physical interface combination is
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}U\_T*Y\_T + U\_w*Y\_w}}. Its vanishing is
a \sphinxstyleemphasis{sum of signed exchanges}, not an assertion
that each exchanged power must be zero.
The heat\sphinxhyphen{}side dissipation is
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{D = integral(e\_Q.e\_Q, Omega\_H) \textgreater{}= 0}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Numerical interpretation matters:} with the
command above, each real accepted CN step has been
saved and the canonical example checks the
per\sphinxhyphen{}step discrete identity of its quadratic
Hamiltonian (for the validated physical weak form).
The long default run \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dt=.001, dt\_save=.05}}
saves \sphinxstylestrong{subsampled} states: it cannot reconstruct
the true CN per\sphinxhyphen{}step stage powers from these
snapshots alone. Its plot uses actual instantaneous
nodal GetFEM powers and an explicitly labelled
\sphinxstylestrong{approximate} trapezoidal cumulative work.
The general SCRIMP API does not promise
an exact port\sphinxhyphen{}Hamiltonian identity for every
PETSc TS method or nonlinear Hamiltonian.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To choose a different user output root:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
python\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}m\PYG{+w}{ }examples.heat\PYGZus{}wave\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}final\PYGZhy{}time\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}.2\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}time\PYGZhy{}step\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}.002\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}save\PYGZhy{}step\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}.002\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}output\PYGZhy{}dir\PYG{+w}{ }/tmp/my\PYGZhy{}heat\PYGZhy{}wave\PYGZhy{}results
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The full output contract, MPI root\sphinxhyphen{}only writer
policy, source tests and native acceptance command
are recorded in
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{docs/V130\_EXAMPLES\_OUTPUT\_CONTRACT.md}}.


\subsubsection{Setting}
\label{\detokenize{examples/heat_wave:setting}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
It is assumed that the \sphinxhref{https://g-haine.github.io/scrimp/examples/wave.html}{2D wave
equation}, the
\sphinxhref{https://g-haine.github.io/scrimp/examples/wave\_coenergy.html}{2D wave equation in co\sphinxhyphen{}energy
formulation}
and the \sphinxhref{https://g-haine.github.io/scrimp/examples/heat.html}{2D heat
equation} have
already been studied.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The objective of this example is to deal with interconnection in the
sense of port\sphinxhyphen{}Hamiltonian systems.

\sphinxAtStartPar
We are interested in the coupled heat\sphinxhyphen{}wave system which can be
formulated as follows: let \(\Omega := \Omega_W \cup \Omega_H\) be a
bounded domain in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) such that
\(\Omega_W \cap \Omega_H = \emptyset\), we denote
\(\Gamma_I := \partial\Omega_W \cap \partial\Omega_H\) the interface
between the two domains, and
\(\Gamma_W := \partial\Omega_W \setminus \Gamma_I\) and
\(\Gamma_H := \partial\Omega_H \setminus \Gamma_I\). The system of
equations reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\lbrace
\begin{array}{rcl}
\partial_t T(t,x) &=& {\rm div}\left( {\rm grad}\left( T(t,x) \right)\right), \quad \forall t\ge0, x \in \Omega_H, \\
\partial_{tt}^2 w(t,x) &=& {\rm div}\left( {\rm grad}\left( w(t,x) \right)\right), \quad \forall t\ge0, x \in \Omega_W, \\
T(t,s) &=& 0, \quad \forall t\ge0, s \in \Gamma_H, \\
w(t,s) &=& 0, \quad \forall t\ge0, s \in \Gamma_W, \\
\end{array}
\right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
together with the transmission conditions across the interface
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\lbrace
\begin{array}{rcl}
T(t,s) &=& \partial_t w(t,s), \quad \forall t\ge0, s \in \Gamma_I, \\
\partial_{n_H} T(t,s) &=& - \partial_{n_W} w(t,s), \quad \forall t\ge0, s \in \Gamma_I, \\
\end{array}
\right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(n_H\) is the outward normal to \(\Omega_H\) and
\(n_W\) is the outward normal to \(\Omega_W\). Hence,
\(n_H = -n_W\) on \(\Gamma_I\).


\subsubsection{Port\sphinxhyphen{}Hamiltonian framework}
\label{\detokenize{examples/heat_wave:port-hamiltonian-framework}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The heat equation

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The heat equation reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{pmatrix} \partial_t T \\ e_q \end{pmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix} 0 & - {\rm div} \\ - {\rm grad} & 0 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} T \\ e_Q \end{pmatrix},\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
together with the boundary ports
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\lbrace
\begin{array}{rcl}
u^I_H &=& T, \quad \Gamma_I, \\
y^I_H &=& e_Q \cdot n_H, \quad \Gamma_I,
\end{array}
\right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\lbrace
\begin{array}{rcl}
u_H &=& T, \quad \Gamma_H, \\
y_H &=& e_Q \cdot n_H, \quad \Gamma_H.
\end{array}
\right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The wave equation

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Dirichlet boundary condition has to be relaxed by
\(\partial_t w = 0\) to fit the port\sphinxhyphen{}Hamiltonian framework.
Providing this adaptation and the notation \(p := \partial_t w\) and
\(q := {\rm grad}\left(w\right)\), the wave equation reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{pmatrix} \partial_t q \\ \partial_t p \end{pmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix} 0 & {\rm grad} \\ {\rm div} & 0 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} q \\ p \end{pmatrix},\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
together with the boundary ports
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\lbrace
\begin{array}{rcl}
u^I_W &=& q \cdot n_W, \quad \Gamma_I, \\
y^I_W &=& p, \quad \Gamma_I,
\end{array}
\right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\lbrace
\begin{array}{rcl}
u_W &=& q \cdot n_W, \quad \Gamma_H, \\
y_W &=& p, \quad \Gamma_H.
\end{array}
\right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The interconnection

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The transmission condition at the interface may be recast as a
power\sphinxhyphen{}preserving interconnection. It can be either a \sphinxstylestrong{gyrator} or a
\sphinxstylestrong{tranformer} interconnection, depending on the chosen causality for
each system. We the above choices, we have a \sphinxstylestrong{gyrator
interconnection}, indeed, one has
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}u^I_H = y^I_w, \qquad u^I_W = y^I_H.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Automatic assembly of conforming interfaces (v1.3.0)

\sphinxAtStartPar
For this \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Concentric}} mesh, SCRIMP automatically resolves the
logical interface region \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{10}} into the two adjacent sets of
facets and assembles each normal\sphinxhyphen{}dependent weak term on its
correct subdomain side, using that side’s outward normal. This
is the default on the v1.3.0 preparation branch. The physical
gyrator relations \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{U\_T = Y\_w}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{U\_w = Y\_T}} remain
part of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{model}, not something inferred from mesh topology.
Unsupported or ambiguous conforming interfaces fail explicitly.
See the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/g-haine/scrimp/blob/release/1.3.0-preparation/docs/V130\_INTERFACE\_PV\_PRODUCTION\_DECISION\_20261124.md}{interface assembly and MPI production policy}
for the scope, geometric orientation and native qualification.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{Structure\sphinxhyphen{}preserving discretization}
\label{\detokenize{examples/heat_wave:structure-preserving-discretization}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The heat equation

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
We use the div\sphinxhyphen{}div formulation already presented in the \sphinxhref{https://g-haine.github.io/scrimp/examples/heat.html}{2D heat
equation}
example, \sphinxstyleemphasis{i.e.} we obtain the following system
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}
M_T & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & M_Q & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & M^I_H & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & M_H
\end{bmatrix}}_{= M}
\begin{pmatrix}
\frac{\rm d}{{\rm d}t} \underline{T}(t) \\
\underline{e_Q}(t) \\
-\underline{y^I_H}(t) \\
-\underline{y_H}(t)
\end{pmatrix}
=
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}
0 & D & 0 & 0 \\
-D^\top & 0 & B^I_H & B_H \\
0 & -(B^I_H)^\top & 0 & 0 \\
0 & -(B_H)^\top & 0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}}_{= J}
\begin{pmatrix}
\underline{T}(t) \\
\underline{e_Q}(t) \\
\underline{u^I_H}(t) \\
\underline{u_H}(t)
\end{pmatrix},\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The wave equation

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
We use the grad\sphinxhyphen{}grad formulation already presented in the \sphinxhref{https://g-haine.github.io/scrimp/examples/wave.html}{2D wave
equation}
example, \sphinxstyleemphasis{i.e.} we obtain the following system
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}
M_q & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & M_p & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & M^I_W & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & M_W
\end{bmatrix}}_{= M}
\begin{pmatrix}
\frac{\rm d}{{\rm d}t} \underline{q}(t) \\
\frac{\rm d}{{\rm d}t} \underline{p}(t) \\
-\underline{y^I_W}(t) \\
\underline{u_W}(t)
\end{pmatrix}
=
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}
0 & D & 0 & 0 \\
-D^\top & 0 & B^I_W & -B_W^\top \\
0 & -(B^I_W)^\top & 0 & 0 \\
0 & B_W & 0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}}_{= J}
\begin{pmatrix}
\underline{q}(t) \\
\underline{p}(t) \\
\underline{u^I_W}(t) \\
-\underline{y_W}(t)
\end{pmatrix},\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The gyrator interconnection

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This condition is easy to implement, and leads to
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}M^I_H \underline{u^I_H}(t) = M^I_W \underline{y^I_W}(t), \qquad M^I_W \underline{u^I_W}(t) = M^I_H \underline{y^I_H}(t).\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Finally, the \sphinxstylestrong{gyrator} interconnection is implemented as reciprocal
output feedback. In SCRIMP v1.3.0, the automatic conforming\sphinxhyphen{}interface
compiler uses the actual \sphinxstylestrong{outward normal of each owning subdomain}.
The two interface powers therefore cancel with the physical signs
\(-U_T Y_T + U_w Y_w=0\); no artificial common\sphinxhyphen{}normal sign flip
must be introduced. See the interface note above for the validated
scope and implementation reference.

    \PYG{n}{S}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Term}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Potential energy}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{0.5*q.q}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{wave\PYGZus{}region}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}

\subsubsection{Long\sphinxhyphen{}time wave gallery exploration (v1.3.0)}
\label{\detokenize{examples/heat_wave:long-time-wave-gallery-exploration-v1-3-0}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The canonical source now generates \sphinxstylestrong{its own}
long\sphinxhyphen{}time energy and wave\sphinxhyphen{}visualization files,
using real GetFEM/PETSc fields. For an annulus
containing the wave equation
(\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{heat\_region=1}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{wave\_region=2}}),
run the reproducible Docker showcase
\sphinxstylestrong{after} separately passing the strict
short\sphinxhyphen{}horizon physical CN gate:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZti{}/Simulations/scrimp
\PYG{n+nv}{SCRIMP\PYGZus{}DOCKER\PYGZus{}NO\PYGZus{}SUDO}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{n+nv}{SCRIMP\PYGZus{}V130\PYGZus{}DAE\PYGZus{}IMAGE}\PYG{o}{=}scrimp\PYGZhy{}mpi:v1.3.0\PYGZhy{}rc3\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
bash\PYG{+w}{ }scripts/run\PYGZhy{}v130\PYGZhy{}heat\PYGZhy{}wave\PYGZhy{}long\PYGZhy{}showcase.sh
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The profile selected by default in this
\sphinxstyleemphasis{showcase} is an angular wave packet
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gallery\_packet}} concentrated near the
outer annulus, with initial oscillation
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cos(14*theta)}}. It is \sphinxstylestrong{not} a computed
waveguide/cavity eigenmode. To generate
the \sphinxstylestrong{original Gaussian} heat\textendash{}wave case
over the same long horizon, use
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SCRIMP\_V130\_HW\_SHOWCASE\_PROFILE=gaussian}}
with the command above.
In both cases, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{initial\_wave\_boundary="clamp"}}
enforces the homogeneous Dirichlet
condition exactly on the filtered
exterior CG1 degrees of freedom, after
the real default L\(\sp{\text{2}}\) projection.
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{constrained\_l2}} is the alternative
true GetFEM\sphinxhyphen{}mass minimizing correction
(MPI1 only). The strict algebraic
initializer is never relaxed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The physical example automatically
writes under \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{outputs/heat\_wave/}} in its typed
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{png/}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{svg/}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gif/}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{npz/}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{json/}} folders:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{heat\_wave\_H\_long\_loglog.png}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.svg}}, together with the native
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{heat\_wave\_FE\_H\_long.npz}} numerical
trajectory (zero time is excluded
\sphinxstylestrong{only} from the log\sphinxhyphen{}log plot);

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
four original FE \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{p}} snapshots
of the outer annulus and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{wave\_annulus\_long.gif}} using
at most 48 genuine saved VTK frames,
with a fixed scalar color scale;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{wave\_outer\_shell\_kinetic\_proxy.png}}
showing an approximate CG1
kinetic\sphinxhyphen{}velocity fraction in
the outer ring \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{r\textgreater{}=0.82}};

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{json/heat\_wave\_long\_showcase.json}} with the
exact selected GetFEM times,
the initial profile, and explicit
qualification limitations.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The exported original \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{T}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{p}}
VTK/PVD time series are
retained under \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{outputs/heat\_wave/mesh/}}
for detailed ParaView inspection. The \sphinxstylestrong{H(t)} curve is an
actual FE Hamiltonian quadrature;
the images show actual native
GetFEM fields at nodes.
The radial diagnostic samples \sphinxstylestrong{only
CG1 kinetic energy}, with a
centroid\sphinxhyphen{}based shell approximation.
It is \sphinxstylestrong{not} the full wave energy,
a modal eigenanalysis, or a
whispering\sphinxhyphen{}gallery proof. Such a
claim would additionally require
persistent near\sphinxhyphen{}boundary localization
and a mode/directional propagation
study. See
\sphinxhref{https://github.com/g-haine/scrimp/blob/release/1.3.0-preparation/docs/V130\_HEAT\_WAVE\_PHYSICAL\_AUDIT.md}{the v1.3.0 Heat\textendash{}Wave physical report}
for the distinct native qualification
and evidence.


\subsubsection{Native qualification: MPI1/2 FE parity and full\sphinxhyphen{}length CN power}
\label{\detokenize{examples/heat_wave:native-qualification-mpi1-2-fe-parity-and-full-length-cn-power}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The short native Heat\textendash{}Wave case has a
true physical \sphinxstylestrong{MUMPS MPI1 PASS}.
The existing 15\sphinxhyphen{}second Gaussian and
annular visualizations are also complete,
but their saved \sphinxstylestrong{0.05} time spacing
does not represent consecutive \sphinxstylestrong{0.005}
Crank\textendash{}Nicolson steps. Therefore the
figures alone cannot certify the
\sphinxstylestrong{heat, wave and coupled energy\sphinxhyphen{}power
identities at every time step}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An additional \sphinxstyleemphasis{independent} native pilot
tests this distinction, without changing
the governing model:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZti{}/Simulations/scrimp
git\PYG{+w}{ }pull\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}ff\PYGZhy{}only
\PYG{n+nv}{SCRIMP\PYGZus{}DOCKER\PYGZus{}NO\PYGZus{}SUDO}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{n+nv}{SCRIMP\PYGZus{}V130\PYGZus{}DAE\PYGZus{}IMAGE}\PYG{o}{=}scrimp\PYGZhy{}mpi:v1.3.0\PYGZhy{}rc3\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
bash\PYG{+w}{ }scripts/run\PYGZhy{}v130\PYGZhy{}heat\PYGZhy{}wave\PYGZhy{}mpi\PYGZhy{}long\PYGZhy{}physics.sh
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Stage A compares \sphinxstylestrong{all 7,689 original FE
coefficients} and independently assembled
heat/wave/interface physical quadratures
between MUMPS MPI1 and MPI2 at each of
five original CN times. It requires
the two MPI2 ranks to agree exactly.
Only after stage A passes does stage B
run \sphinxstylestrong{3,000} genuine MUMPS MPI1 CN
steps through \sphinxtitleref{t\_f=15},
\sphinxstylestrong{saving all 3,001 states} so that
each midpoint power is evaluated on the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{actual adjacent FE states}, not on
widely separated visualization snapshots.
The native code also tests the cumulative
energy\sphinxhyphen{}power balance. The default
Gaussian profile can be compared to
the separate 15\sphinxhyphen{}second visual archive;
the optional environment variable
\sphinxtitleref{SCRIMP\_V130\_HW\_LONG\_PROFILE=gallery\_packet}
tests the angular\sphinxhyphen{}packet physics
independently.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only the new \sphinxtitleref{physics\_only=True}
output option suppresses PNG/PVD
writers during the MPI calculation:
the canonical PDE, FEM, boundary
clamp, strict DAE initializer, native
PETSc solve and GetFEM quadratures
remain unchanged. The ordinary
tutorial still creates all its
plots and ParaView output by default.
Every native run and failure gets a
complete evidence ZIP.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Qualification completed 25 November 2026.}
The actual native source \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{97c7606b}}
(\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scrimp\sphinxhyphen{}mpi:v1.3.0\sphinxhyphen{}rc3}},
MUMPS) has passed both phases:

The original GetFEM 5.5 field exporter writes an \sphinxstyleemphasis{IEEE Float32}
