\subsubsection{Setting}
\label{\detokenize{examples/shallow_water:setting}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The objective of this example is to show how to deal with
\sphinxstylestrong{non\sphinxhyphen{}linearity}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let us consider a bounded domain \(\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2\).
The shallow water equations are constituted of two conservation laws
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{pmatrix}
\partial_t h \\ \partial_t p
\end{pmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix}
0 & - {\rm div} \\
-{\rm grad} & \frac{1}{h} G(\omega)
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
{e}_h \\ {e_p}
\end{pmatrix} ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(h\) is the height of the fluid, \(v\) is the velocity,
\(\rho\) is the fluid density (supposed constant),
\(p := \rho v\) is the linear momentum,
\(\omega := {\rm curl}_{2D} \left( v \right) := \partial_x v_y - \partial_y v_x\)
is the vorticity,
\(G(\omega):=\rho \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\,{\omega}\),
\(e_h = \frac{1}{2} \rho\,\|v\|^2 + \rho g h\) is the total pressure
and \(e_p = h v\) is the volumetric flow of the fluid. Thus, the
first line of the matrix equation represents the conservation of the
mass (or volume, since the fluid is assumed to be incompressible) and
the second represents the conservation of linear momentum.


\subsubsection{Port\sphinxhyphen{}Hamiltonian framework}
\label{\detokenize{examples/shallow_water:port-hamiltonian-framework}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
One can define the system Hamiltonian (or total energy) as a functional
of \(h\) and \(p\), which are thus called energy variables
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathcal{H} (h,p) := \frac{1}{2} \int_\Omega \frac{h(t,x) \| p(t,x) \|^2}{\rho} + \rho g h^2(t,x) {\rm d}x.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The co\sphinxhyphen{}energy variables can be computed from the variational derivative
of the Hamiltonian such that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{split}
    e_h & = \delta_h \mathcal{H} = \frac{1}{2} \rho \| v \|^2 +  \rho g h , \\
    e_p & = \delta_{p} \mathcal{H} = h v .
\end{split}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The time\sphinxhyphen{}derivative of the Hamiltonian can then be obtained computed and
depends only on the boundary variables
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{\rm d}{{\rm d}t} \mathcal{H} =  - \int_{\partial\Omega} e_h(t,s) e_p(t,s) \cdot n(s) {\rm d}s ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
which enables to define collocated control and observation distributed
ports along the boundary \(\partial\Omega\). For example, one may
define
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{split}
     u_{\partial} & = - e_p \cdot n,\\
     y_{\partial} & = e_h,
 \end{split}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and the power\sphinxhyphen{}balance is given by a product between input and output
boundary ports. The system is lossless, and conservative in the absence
of control.


\subsubsection{Structure\sphinxhyphen{}preserving discretization}
\label{\detokenize{examples/shallow_water:structure-preserving-discretization}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
First, let us multiply the linear momentum conservation equation by
\(h\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let us consider sufficiently regular test functions \(\varphi\) and
\(\Phi\) on \(\Omega\), and \(\psi\) test functions at the
boundary \(\partial\Omega\). The weak form of the previous equations
reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\lbrace
\begin{array}{rcl}
\left( \partial_t h, \varphi \right)_{L^2} &=& - \left( {\rm div}\left( h e_p \right), \varphi \right)_{L^2}, \\
\left( h \partial_t p, \Phi \right)_{(L^2)^2} &=& - \left( h {\rm grad}\left( e_h \right), \Phi \right)_{(L^2)^2}
                        + \left( {\rm curl}_{2D}\left( p \right) \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} e_p, \Phi \right)_{(L^2)^2}, \\
\left( y_\partial, \psi \right)_{\partial\Omega} &=& \left( e_h, \psi \right)_{\partial\Omega}.
\end{array}
\right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Applying integration by parts on the first line leads to
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\lbrace
\begin{array}{rcl}
\left( \partial_t h, \varphi \right)_{L^2} &=& \left( h e_p, {\rm grad} \left( \varphi \right) \right)_{L^2} + \left( h u_\partial, \varphi \right)_{\partial\Omega}, \\
\left( h \partial_t p, \Phi \right)_{(L^2)^2} &=& - \left( h {\rm grad} \left( e_h \right), \Phi \right)_{(L^2)^2}
                        + \left( {\rm curl}_{2D}\left( p \right) \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} e_p, \Phi \right)_{(L^2)^2}, \\
\left( y_\partial, \psi \right)_{\partial\Omega} &=& \left( e_h, \psi \right)_{\partial\Omega}.
\end{array}
\right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Furthermore, the weak form of the constitutive relations write
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\lbrace
\begin{array}{rcl}
\left( e_h, \varphi \right)_{L^2} &=& \left( \rho g h, \varphi \right)_{L^2} + \left( \frac{\| p \|^2}{2 \rho}, \varphi \right)_{L^2}, \\
\left( e_p, \Phi \right)_{(L^2)^2} &=& \left( \frac{p}{\rho}, \Phi \right)_{(L^2)^2}.
\end{array}
\right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Now, let us choose three finite families
\((\varphi^i)_{1 \le i \le N_h} \subset H^1(\Omega)\),
\((\Phi^k)_{1 \le k \le N_p} \subset (L^2(\Omega))^2\) and
\((\psi^m)_{1 \le m \le N_\partial}\) and project the weak
formulations on them: for all \(1 \le i \le N_h\), all
\(1 \le k \le N_p\) and all \(1 \le m \le N_\partial\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\lbrace
\begin{array}{rcl}
\sum_{j=1}^{N_h} \frac{\rm d}{{\rm d}t} h^j \left( \varphi^j, \varphi^i \right)_{L^2} &=& \sum_{\ell=1}^{N_p} e_p^\ell \left( h^d \Phi^\ell, {\rm grad} \left( \varphi^i \right) \right)_{L^2} + \sum_{n=1}^{N_\partial} u_\partial^n \left( h^d \psi^n, \varphi^i \right)_{\partial\Omega}, \\
\sum_{\ell=1}^{N_p} \frac{\rm d}{{\rm d}t} p^\ell \left( h^d \Phi^\ell, \Phi^k \right)_{(L^2)^2} &=& - \sum_{j=1}^{N_h} e_h^j \left( h^d {\rm grad} \left( \varphi^j \right), \Phi^k \right)_{(L^2)^2} \\
                       && \quad + \sum_{\ell=1}^{N_p} e_p^\ell \left( {\rm curl}_{2D}\left( p^d \right) \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \Phi^\ell, \Phi^k \right)_{(L^2)^2}, \\
\sum_{n=1}^{N_\partial} y_\partial^n \left( \psi^n, \psi^m \right)_{\partial\Omega} &=& \sum_{j=1}^{N_h} e_h^j \left( \varphi^j, \psi^m \right)_{\partial\Omega},
\end{array}
\right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(h^d := \sum_{i=1}^{N_h} h^i \varphi^i\) is the approximation
of \(h\) and \(p^d := \sum_{k=1}^{N_p} p^k \Phi^k\) is the
approximation of \(p\). The constitutive relations read for all
\(1 \le i \le N_h\) and all \(1 \le k \le N_p\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\lbrace
\begin{array}{rcl}
\sum_{j=1}^{N_h} e_h^j \left( \varphi^j, \varphi^i \right)_{L^2} &=& \sum_{j=1}^{N_h} h^j \left( \rho g \varphi^j, \varphi^i \right)_{L^2} + \sum_{\ell=1}^{N_p} p^\ell \left( \frac{\Phi^\ell \cdot p^d}{2 \rho}, \varphi^i \right)_{L^2}, \\
\sum_{\ell=1}^{N_p} e_p^\ell \left( \Phi^\ell, \Phi^k \right)_{(L^2)^2} &=& \sum_{\ell=1}^{N_p} p^\ell \left( \frac{\Phi^\ell}{\rho}, \Phi^k \right)_{(L^2)^2}.
\end{array}
\right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Defining \(\underline{\star}\) the vector gathering the coefficient
of the approximation of the variable \(\star\) in its appropriate
finite family, one may write the discrete weak formulations in matrix
notation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{bmatrix} M_h & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & M_p[h^d] & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & M_\partial \end{bmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \underline{h} \\ \underline{p} \\ -\underline{y_\partial} \end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & D[h^d] & B[h^d] \\
-D[h^d]^\top & G[p^d] & 0 \\
- B^\top & 0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} \underline{e_h} \\ \underline{e_p} \\ \underline{u_\partial} \end{pmatrix}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where the matrices are given by
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}(M_h)_{ij} := \left( \varphi^j, \varphi^i \right)_{L^2} \qquad (M_p[h^d])_{k\ell} := \left( h^d \Phi^\ell, \Phi^k \right)_{(L^2)^2},\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}(D[h^d])_{i\ell} := \left( h^d \Phi^\ell, {\rm grad} \left( \varphi^i \right) \right)_{L^2}, \qquad (B[h^d])_{in} := \left( h^d \psi^n, \varphi^i \right)_{\partial\Omega},\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}(M_\partial)_{mn} := \left( \psi^n, \psi^m \right)_{\partial\Omega}, \qquad (B)_{in} := \left( \psi^n, \varphi^i \right)_{\partial\Omega}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The constitutive relations read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{bmatrix} M_h & 0 \\ 0 & M_p \end{bmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \underline{e_h} \\ \underline{e_p} \end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
Q_h & P_h[h^d] \\
0 & Q_p
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} \underline{h} \\ \underline{p} \end{pmatrix},\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where the matrices are given by
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}(M_p)_{k\ell} := \left( \Phi^\ell, \Phi^k \right)_{(L^2)^2}, \qquad (Q_h)_{ij} := \left( \rho g \varphi^j, \varphi^i \right)_{L^2},\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}(P_h[h^d])_{i\ell} := \left( \frac{\Phi^\ell \cdot p^d}{2 \rho}, \varphi^i \right)_{L^2}, \qquad (Q_d)_{k\ell} := \left( \frac{\Phi^\ell}{\rho}, \Phi^k \right)_{(L^2)^2}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
With these definition, one may prove the \sphinxstylestrong{discrete power balance}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{\rm d}{{\rm d}t} \mathcal{H}^d(t) = \underline{u_\partial}^\top(t) M_\partial \underline{y_\partial}(t).\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here are the difficult part. We need to define the weak form of each
block matrices, and take non\sphinxhyphen{}linearities into account. To do so, the
GFWL of GetFEM is transparent, but it is mandatory to say to \sphinxstylestrong{SCRIMP}
that the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Brick}} is non\sphinxhyphen{}linear, using the keyword \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{linear=False}}. It
is also possible to ask for a nonlinear weak\sphinxhyphen{}form brick to be
\sphinxstylestrong{fully explicit}: SCRIMP evaluates its entire weak\sphinxhyphen{}form contribution
at the \sphinxstylestrong{last accepted time/state} \((t_n,z_n)\) before starting
the following PETSc TS step. The resulting distributed PETSc RHS is
then held fixed during \sphinxstylestrong{all} Newton and line\sphinxhyphen{}search trials at
\(t_{n+1}\). In particular, this term has zero derivative with
respect to the implicit trial state and is absent from the Jacobian.
The gyroscopic \sphinxtitleref{G} term below uses \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{explicit=True}} for this
purpose.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is deliberately a \sphinxstylestrong{one\sphinxhyphen{}step lag}, not a partially implicit
evaluation with a current Newton trial effort. Its time accuracy
is generally \sphinxstylestrong{first order}, even if the implicit subsystem uses
BDF2. In addition, the skew\sphinxhyphen{}symmetry of the instantaneous
gyroscopic operator does \sphinxstylestrong{not} by itself guarantee exact
discrete Hamiltonian conservation when the entire G term is
evaluated at the previous state. Exact discrete energy preservation
requires a suitable implicit/midpoint or specialized geometric split.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The v1.3.0 fully explicit mode supports \sphinxstylestrong{nonlinear \textasciigrave{}dt=False\textasciigrave{}
non\sphinxhyphen{}source weak forms}. Other explicit bricks raise a clear
error rather than silently entering the implicit matrix.
The original gyroscopic weak\sphinxhyphen{}form expression and sign
are preserved.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{important}{Important:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The gyroscopic brick \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{G}} above has
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{explicit=True}}: SCRIMP evaluates it at the \sphinxstylestrong{last
accepted} time/state and freezes its contribution during
all Newton and line\sphinxhyphen{}search iterations of the next step.
Its derivative is excluded from the implicit Jacobian,
as is mathematically consistent with that \sphinxstyleemphasis{genuinely
explicit} discretization. This creates a generally
\sphinxstylestrong{first\sphinxhyphen{}order lag for G}, even though the implicit
integrator here is BDF2. Exact Hamiltonian conservation
is not automatically guaranteed by this split.
See {\hyperref[\detokenize{explicit_bricks::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Fully explicit nonlinear bricks}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{state\sphinxhyphen{}dependent\sphinxhyphen{}mass Jacobian} of the original
shallow\sphinxhyphen{}water weak forms has been independently
qualified by a native MPI 1/2 full\sphinxhyphen{}residual directional
finite\sphinxhyphen{}difference test (20 November 2026):
default corrected maximum relative error
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{1.06105781e\sphinxhyphen{}8}}, historical \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{legacy}}
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{3.84378444e\sphinxhyphen{}6}} (unchanged \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{1e\sphinxhyphen{}5}}
acceptance threshold). The test freezes a nonzero
explicit \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{G}}, but does \sphinxstylestrong{not} integrate a
physical time step. Separate short native BDF2 physical
simulations and a fixed\sphinxhyphen{}final\sphinxhyphen{}time refinement campaign have
since been performed with strict nonlinear\sphinxhyphen{}affine algebraic
initialization. They measured the energy defect without
claiming exact conservation; the extended native pilot
below adds full FE rank parity and a longer physical horizon.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\subsubsection{Extended native physical validation (SCRIMP v1.3.0)}
\label{\detokenize{examples/shallow_water:extended-native-physical-validation-scrimp-v1-3-0}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The canonical 2\sphinxhyphen{}D \sphinxstylestrong{inviscid} shallow\sphinxhyphen{}water example is distinct
from the viscous, rotating disk experiment. Its nonlinear
state\sphinxhyphen{}dependent momentum mass has already passed a true
GetFEM/PETSc directional finite\sphinxhyphen{}difference Jacobian test
in MPI 1/2. The model’s \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{nonlinear\_affine}} initializer has
also passed separate native compatibility tests, along with
short original BDF2 physical\sphinxhyphen{}time trajectories.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An additional \sphinxstylestrong{bounded native acceptance pilot} now runs the
unchanged rectangular model, original initial data and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{explicit=True}} gyroscopic term to
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{t\_f=0.002}}, at \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dt=0.0001}} (20 steps) and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dt=0.00005}} (40 steps), both in MPI 1 and MPI 2:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZti{}/Simulations/scrimp
git\PYG{+w}{ }pull\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}ff\PYGZhy{}only
conda\PYG{+w}{ }activate\PYG{+w}{ }scrimp

\PYG{n+nv}{SCRIMP\PYGZus{}DOCKER\PYGZus{}NO\PYGZus{}SUDO}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{n+nv}{SCRIMP\PYGZus{}V130\PYGZus{}DAE\PYGZus{}IMAGE}\PYG{o}{=}scrimp\PYGZhy{}mpi:v1.3.0\PYGZhy{}rc3\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
bash\PYG{+w}{ }scripts/run\PYGZhy{}v130\PYGZhy{}shallow\PYGZhy{}water\PYGZhy{}extended\PYGZhy{}physical.sh
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The diagnostic, not the default public entry point, explicitly
selects \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{init\_step\_ts\_type="nonlinear\_affine"}}
to preserve the \sphinxstylestrong{original prescribed} differential initial
data exactly. It records the true FE coefficients on every
MPI rank and independently checks mass, Hamiltonian, all
four boundary\sphinxhyphen{}port powers and the measured BDF2 defect
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{H(T)\sphinxhyphen{}H(0)\sphinxhyphen{}integrated\_boundary\_work}}.
It \sphinxstylestrong{does not} impose machine\sphinxhyphen{}precision conservation on
an integrator with a lagged explicit term, nor claim
a temporal convergence order from two refinements
of a discontinuous initial free surface.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The standard \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{shallow\_water\_eq()}} still uses the
historical pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}time initialization and final time
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{0.5}} by default. The bounded pilot does \sphinxstylestrong{not}
qualify that full default trajectory or the separate
high\sphinxhyphen{}index rotating viscous Saint\sphinxhyphen{}Venant model.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Native qualification PASS (25 November 2026):}
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PASS\_SWE\_BOUNDED\_NATIVE\_BDF2\_MPI1\_MPI2}}.
All four original GetFEM/PETSc simulations finished:
20 and 40 BDF2 steps, both MPI 1 and MPI 2, no rejected
step or nonlinear solver failure, with \sphinxstylestrong{4,270 original
finite element unknowns} and the full FE solution saved
at all 21 or 41 accepted instants.

\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{1.9758294457}} and two\sphinxhyphen{}point log2 exponent
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{0.9824584184}}. This is \sphinxstylestrong{an observed energy\sphinxhyphen{}defect
trend only}. The original explicit previous\sphinxhyphen{}state
gyroscopic splitting is not exactly energy\sphinxhyphen{}preserving,
and two resolutions with discontinuous initial water
height cannot establish an asymptotic convergence order
or exact long\sphinxhyphen{}time conservation.

\subsubsection{Original inviscid free\sphinxhyphen{}surface visualizations (v1.3.0, direct example run)}
\label{\detokenize{examples/shallow_water:original-inviscid-free-surface-visualizations-v1-3-0-direct-example-run}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The shallow\sphinxhyphen{}water \sphinxstylestrong{example} also has a genuine, opt\sphinxhyphen{}in visual
mode. \sphinxstylestrong{All source code for this example, including the native VTK
reader and image/GIF generation, is inside the single
\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}examples/shallow\_water.py\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{} file.} There is no separate
example visualization module to import or maintain. A helper in
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scripts/}} can optionally recover images from existing VTK
archives without running the nonlinear solve, but it is not needed
for the public example.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is \sphinxstylestrong{not} the separately studied, viscous rotating
Saint\textendash{}Venant research model (with or without feedback),
associated with MCSS and LHMNC 2027.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Running the example itself now generates its visualizations by
default.} No separate rendering script, postprocessing command or
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}showcase}} argument is necessary. On a working SCRIMP/GetFEM
installation, launch the canonical single file:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZti{}/Simulations/scrimp
conda\PYG{+w}{ }activate\PYG{+w}{ }scrimp
python\PYG{+w}{ }examples/shallow\PYGZus{}water.py
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The equivalent command is
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{python \sphinxhyphen{}m examples.shallow\_water}}. The direct entry point
runs the true inviscid BDF2 model with MUMPS MPI1,
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{t\_f=0.12}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dt=0.0001}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dt\_save=0.002}},
and production \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{nonlinear\_affine}} initialization, then
exports the native \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{h}} (CG2) and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{p}} (DG1) VTUs and creates
\sphinxstylestrong{all figures automatically, in the same example file}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The default output location is determined by the current directory:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
outputs/shallow\PYGZus{}water/
├── png/
│   ├── saint\PYGZus{}venant\PYGZus{}champs\PYGZus{}t*.png
│   ├── saint\PYGZus{}venant\PYGZus{}H\PYGZus{}masse\PYGZus{}bilan.png

The program prints the resulting paths. Use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}showcase\sphinxhyphen{}output PATH}}
if another output directory is wanted, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}final\sphinxhyphen{}time}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}time\sphinxhyphen{}step}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}save\sphinxhyphen{}step}} to change the simulation
horizon/resolution. The historical original \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pseudo}} initializer,

programmatic behavior. The default \sphinxstylestrong{executable} behavior is

For additional pinned\sphinxhyphen{}Docker scientific acceptance,
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scripts/run\sphinxhyphen{}v130\sphinxhyphen{}shallow\sphinxhyphen{}water\sphinxhyphen{}showcase.sh}} calls this
\sphinxstylestrong{same example} with explicit arguments and archives its
original outputs. It is \sphinxstyleemphasis{not} necessary to generate the figures.

\begin{itemize}

Three synchronized views in

the 2\sphinxhyphen{}D free surface represented as a \sphinxstylestrong{3\sphinxhyphen{}D

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Four native GetFEM h/p PNG snapshots
spanning the simulation, with fixed

\item {}

All spatial views use the actual
GetFEM\sphinxhyphen{}exported FE values. The per\sphinxhyphen{}triangle

The original run exported 61 genuine VTK
states per field (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{h}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{p}})

\section{Finite\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional port\sphinxhyphen{}Hamiltonian systems}
\label{\detokenize{lumped:finite-dimensional-port-hamiltonian-systems}}\label{\detokenize{lumped::doc}}

\subsection{Global scalar ports (tested examples)}
\label{\detokenize{lumped:global-scalar-ports-tested-examples}}\label{\detokenize{lumped:lumped}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
SCRIMP’s {\hyperref[\detokenize{scrimp:scrimp.dphs.DPHS}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scrimp.dphs.DPHS}}}}} supports \sphinxstylestrong{global scalar
states} and co\sphinxhyphen{}states in addition to distributed finite\sphinxhyphen{}element fields.
The canonical mass\textendash{}spring\textendash{}damper and nonlinear pendulum examples
have passed genuine native PETSc time integration and user\sphinxhyphen{}output
qualification in their documented configurations. This does
\sphinxstylestrong{not} qualify arbitrary coupled PDE\textendash{}ODE constraints, which
remain an experimental extension.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For instance, a mass\textendash{}spring\textendash{}damper has two energy states, displacement
\(q(t)\) and momentum \(p(t)\), and no spatial dependence.
The corresponding energy is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}H(q,p) = \tfrac{k}{2} q^2 + \tfrac{1}{2m} p^2.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There must be exactly \sphinxstylestrong{one degree of freedom} for each variable,
independent of the number of elements in any mesh used elsewhere.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{import}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{scrimp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{as}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{S}

\PYG{n}{sys} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{S}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{DPHS}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{real}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{sys}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{set\PYGZus{}domain}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{S}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Domain}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Interval}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{L}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{h}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{q} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{S}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{State}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{q}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Displacement}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{lumped}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{sys}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}state}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{q}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{sys}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}costate}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{S}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{CoState}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{e\PYGZus{}q}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Elastic effort}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{q}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{sys}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}lumped\PYGZus{}port}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{q}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{sys}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{set\PYGZus{}initial\PYGZus{}value}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{q}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.3}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A global variable is registered with GetFEM’s constant\sphinxhyphen{}size
\sphinxtitleref{Model.add\_variable(name, 1)}, not with \sphinxtitleref{add\_fem\_variable}.
The method {\hyperref[\detokenize{scrimp:scrimp.dphs.DPHS.add_lumped_port}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scrimp.dphs.DPHS.add\_lumped\_port()}}}}} is used \sphinxstylestrong{instead
of} \sphinxtitleref{add\_FEM} for such ports.


\subsection{Global algebraic variables}
\label{\detokenize{lumped:global-algebraic-variables}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
An algebraic variable such as the tank velocity \(v(t)\) can also
be registered as a single degree of freedom:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{sys}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}port}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{S}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Port}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{velocity}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{v}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{unused}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{lumped}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
                    \PYG{n}{algebraic}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{True}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{substituted}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{True}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{sys}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}lumped\PYGZus{}port}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{velocity}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A \sphinxtitleref{substituted=True} algebraic port registers only the flow variable,
which can participate in nonlinear constitutive relations. The flow
has no time derivative and needs no initial value through
\sphinxtitleref{set\_initial\_value}. Dynamic substituted co\sphinxhyphen{}states are not supported
by this initial implementation.


\subsection{Why do bricks use a spatial domain?}
\label{\detokenize{lumped:why-do-bricks-use-a-spatial-domain}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
SCRIMP’s existing bricks are assembled using GetFEM weak forms. To
reuse those same operators for global variables, the example integrates
the scalar residual over a convenient \sphinxstylestrong{reference interval} of length
\(L\), dividing by its measure:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\int_0^L (\dot q-e_p)\,\frac{\mathrm dx}{L}=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\dot q=e_p.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In SCRIMP, these two contributions are represented as

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{S}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Brick}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{M\PYGZus{}q}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{q*Test\PYGZus{}q/L}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{dt}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{True}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{position}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{flow}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{S}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Brick}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{J\PYGZus{}qp}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{e\PYGZus{}p*Test\PYGZus{}q/L}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{position}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{effort}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here \sphinxtitleref{L} is a GetFEM macro defined by the user. This reference
interval is an \sphinxstylestrong{implementation detail}, not a physical continuum
model for the oscillator. There is \sphinxstylestrong{no mesh refinement to perform}
for these 0D examples.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In a \sphinxstylestrong{coupled PDE\textendash{}ODE} system, integration also enables a true
nonlocal constraint. In the experimental sloshing tank, for example,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}M_T v + \int_0^L m(x,t)\,\mathrm dx - P = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
is assembled by the single weak\sphinxhyphen{}form contribution

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{S}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Brick}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{velocity\PYGZus{}constraint}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
        \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{(mom+(Mt*v\PYGZhy{}P)/L)*Test\PYGZus{}v}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
where \sphinxtitleref{mom} is a spatially distributed finite\sphinxhyphen{}element field.
Only one global row is assembled for \sphinxtitleref{v}.


\subsection{Solver and present limits}
\label{\detokenize{lumped:solver-and-present-limits}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The extension updates GetFEM at each PETSc Newton trial iterate,
which is required for implicit nonlinear PDE\textendash{}ODE coupling.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For systems with global scalar ports \sphinxstylestrong{and a linear time\sphinxhyphen{}derivative
mass matrix}, the fully implicit residual takes the form
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}F(t,z,\dot z)=M\dot z + K_{\mathrm{lin}}z
             - \mathrm{rhs}_{\mathrm{GetFEM}}(z,t).\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The nonlinear tangent is used for the Jacobian, not multiplied by
the trial state when reconstructing the residual. This distinction
matters for external forcing and nonlinear constitutive laws.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The global\sphinxhyphen{}port backend has been exercised on a sloshing\sphinxhyphen{}tank
PDE\textendash{}ODE prototype, but this does not constitute full validation.
Boundary conditions, convergence of spatial fields and the
original state\sphinxhyphen{}dependent nonlinear mass\sphinxhyphen{}matrix path remain open
issues. Do not infer that all PDE\textendash{}ODE couplings are supported.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To begin with, you’ll need to install jupyter.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It can be done in the scrimp environment with:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxtitleref{conda activate scrimp}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxtitleref{conda install jupyter ipykernel}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxtitleref{python \sphinxhyphen{}m ipykernel install \textendash{}user \textendash{}name scrimp \textendash{}display\sphinxhyphen{}name “Python (scrimp)”}

\end{enumerate}


\subsection{Run jupyter}
\label{\detokenize{notebooks:run-jupyter}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxtitleref{jupyter notebook \&}

\section{Graphical user interface (experimental)}
\label{\detokenize{GUI:graphical-user-interface-experimental}}\label{\detokenize{GUI::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The graphical interface is \sphinxstylestrong{not currently part of the qualified
v1.3.0 user workflow}. Older SCRIMP versions included a graphical
script generator, but its complete GUI\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}source\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}native\sphinxhyphen{}simulation
path has not yet passed the same release acceptance gates as the
Python examples. In particular, the published 1.3.0 interface must
not promise that every GUI\sphinxhyphen{}generated model and time scheme has
already been validated.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a reproducible introduction, begin with
{\hyperref[\detokenize{started::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Getting started}}}} and the directly executable
{\hyperref[\detokenize{examples::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Examples}}}}. The examples demonstrate the same public
port\sphinxhyphen{}Hamiltonian constructs using real PETSc/GetFEM solvers
and generate their own plots and data under
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{outputs/\textless{}system\_name\textgreater{}/}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The GUI may be explored as an experimental feature only,
with its generated source reviewed before numerical use.
Independent validation of GUI startup, generated scripts,
error reporting and MPI output handling remains a
separate release\sphinxhyphen{}scope decision; it is \sphinxstylestrong{not} silently
treated as covered by the eight canonical example smokes.

\sphinxstepscope

\paragraph{Wave}
\label{\detokenize{scrimp.examples:wave}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Conservative 2D anisotropic membrane with mixed boundary ports.

\sphinxAtStartPar
2D mixed\sphinxhyphen{}boundary anisotropic membrane, energy variables q=grad w,
p=rho*w\_t, coenergy e\_q=T q and e\_p=p/rho. This preserves the
original model’s four boundary ports and its actual GetFEM GWFL
Hamiltonian 0.5*q.T.q, where T is the full tensor parameter.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Physical outward\sphinxhyphen{}normal traction: u\_N=n.e\_q at bottom/right/top;
observation y\_N=e\_p. Left side prescribes u\_D=e\_p (velocity) and
observes y\_D=n.e\_q (traction). The pH energy balance is
\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
H(t)\sphinxhyphen{}H(0) = integral (u\_N*y\_N + u\_D*y\_D) dt.
\end{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The negative flow\sphinxhyphen{}side algebraic rows impose Y\_N=e\_p and U\_D=e\_p:
this is the same physical sign convention as qualified wave\_1d.py.
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{physical} sign of the measured work is audited independently
against the original GetFEM Hamiltonian; no success is inferred
solely from these formulae.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This tutorial starts from EXACTLY zero, compatible with zero
initial Dirichlet velocity and initial normal stress, and uses
a left\sphinxhyphen{}boundary velocity that is zero at t=0 but nontrivial soon
after. The original model, before promotion, passed real MUMPS MPI1/2
10\sphinxhyphen{}step TSCN physical and shared\sphinxhyphen{}ParaView tests at cf42089d;
other LU backends require independent native acceptance.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Scientific context: Haine, Matignon, Serhani (2023), anisotropic
heterogeneous wave PFEM, DOI 10.4208/ijnam2023\sphinxhyphen{}1005; and
Brugnoli, Haine, Matignon (2022) on mixed boundary control.

{\sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{system}}}
{}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Audit actual CN midpoint FE work, damping and boundary feedback.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here the signed algebraic boundary power U*Y is a LOSS: because
the coenergy Grad\sphinxhyphen{}Grad coupling imposes Y=\sphinxhyphen{}p (weakly), the original
FE balance is dH/dt=\sphinxhyphen{}integral(U*Y)\sphinxhyphen{}D\_r. The passive law is U=+kY.
This is not the mixed\sphinxhyphen{}boundary 2A/2B sign convention.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The substituted resistive port has \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} independent flow unknown and
Port.get\_power() correctly cannot report its dissipative power.
We assemble its true mixed FE dissipation in two mathematically
equivalent ways: D\_r=integral e\_r**2/nu = \sphinxhyphen{}integral p*e\_r.
The pointwise nu*p**2 is ONLY a diagnostic because e\_r is DG1 and
nu*p is not generally in the same FE space.

\end{fulllineitems}

\sphinxAtStartPar
q=e\_q (stress), p=e\_p (velocity); Tinv=T**(\sphinxhyphen{}1), rho as in 2A/2B.
Damping acts only on the inner disk, feedback only on the outer rim.
The short fixed CN scenario is for native acceptance, NOT convergence.

{}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
A physically oriented, energy\sphinxhyphen{}dissipative coupled heat\sphinxhyphen{}wave example.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Reference: Haine, Matignon \& Monteghetti, Mathematical Reports (2022),
eqs. (2.1)\sphinxhyphen{}(2.2), (3.15), (4.3)\sphinxhyphen{}(4.5). This example is NOT the paper’s
numerical experiment: it keeps the original SCRIMP heat div\sphinxhyphen{}div and
wave grad\sphinxhyphen{}grad weak forms, choosing compatible mixed FEM spaces.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The original built\sphinxhyphen{}in Concentric geometry has disk=1, annulus=2,
interface=10, outer boundary=20. CN and the 0\sphinxhyphen{}input external
Dirichlet condition are used to expose the heat dissipation and
closed interconnection in an interpretable power balance.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Interface normals always mean each subdomain’s outward normal.
The conservative two\sphinxhyphen{}sided conforming interface compiler is
enabled by default in the v1.3.0 release\sphinxhyphen{}preparation source.
Physical labels, FEM declarations and weak forms are unchanged.
Ambiguous or unsupported interfaces fail explicitly; use
SCRIMP\_AUTO\_INTERFACE=0 only to recover legacy manual assembly
if your model was already oriented by hand.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{heat\_region}} \textendash{} Domain label of the heat equation (1 or 2).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{wave\_region}} \textendash{} Domain label of the wave equation (the other one).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{factor\_solver}} \textendash{} Optional PETSc LU solver (default: SCRIMP MUMPS).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{final\_time}} \textendash{} Physical end time.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{time\_step}} \textendash{} Fixed Crank\textendash{}Nicolson time step.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{save\_step}} \textendash{} Accepted trajectory sampling interval.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{initial\_wave\_profile}} \textendash{} “gaussian” retains the historical heat/wave
condition. “gallery\_packet” is a smooth high\sphinxhyphen{}angular\sphinxhyphen{}wavenumber
wave excitation concentrated near the outer radius, with
zero initial heat and stress. It is \sphinxstylestrong{not} a certified cavity
eigenmode and is available only for a wave annulus.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{long\_showcase}} \textendash{} Produce an opt\sphinxhyphen{}in native GetFEM annular\sphinxhyphen{}wave PNG/GIF
showcase after successful physical integration and VTK export.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{physics\_only}} \textendash{} Run the same full native PDE and initialize the
original Hamiltonian terms but skip plots and ParaView files.
This allows genuine parallel physics audits on all MPI ranks
without concurrent writers; defaults to False and changes
no equations, FEM or physical initialization.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{initial\_wave\_boundary}} \textendash{} Compatible wave velocity initialization
when the exterior boundary belongs to the wave region. “clamp”
(default) sets exactly the exterior CG1 degrees of freedom to zero,
leaving interior L2\sphinxhyphen{}projected coefficients unchanged.
“constrained\_l2” computes the closest zero\sphinxhyphen{}trace field in the
physical GetFEM L2 norm (MPI1 only). “unconstrained” reproduces
the historical, generally DAE\sphinxhyphen{}incompatible Gaussian for diagnostics.
Neither valid method relaxes algebraic DAE constraints.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{output\_dir}} \textendash{} Optional explicit user output directory.

\end{itemize}

\end{description}\end{quote}

A structure\sphinxhyphen{}preserving discretization of the inviscid shallow\sphinxhyphen{}water equation

\sphinxAtStartPar
Formulation Grad\sphinxhyphen{}Grad, homogeneous boundary condition, on a tank.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The executable entry point (python examples/shallow\_water.py or
python \sphinxhyphen{}m examples.shallow\_water) enables showcase=True by DEFAULT:
it solves the genuine inviscid equations and saves original CG2 h,
DG1 p, 3\sphinxhyphen{}D height and velocity PNG/GIF, Hamiltonian and mass plots.
It uses the separately qualified nonlinear\_affine DAE initializer,
leaving the PDE, h/p initial data, four zero controls, mesh, FEM,
BDF2 and lagged gyro unchanged. Default CLI horizon: t\_f=0.12.
For historical compatibility, calling shallow\_water\_eq(showcase=False)
or passing \textendash{}no\sphinxhyphen{}showcase on the CLI retains the old pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}time
initialization and single Hamiltonian / h PVD outputs (t\_f=0.5).
Visual images do not certify exact BDF2 energy conservation.

The original GetFEM 5.5 field exporter writes an \sphinxstyleemphasis{IEEE Float32}
count header for PointData (e.g. h: 547 points \sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{} float32(547),
p: 744 3\sphinxhyphen{}component VTK points from 1488 native 2D scalars \sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}
float32(1488)). The same exporter uses a conventional UInt32
BYTE\sphinxhyphen{}count header for Points and Cells. Both encodings are
independently verified on the native source\sphinxhyphen{}14181a94 archive.
Do not silently parse all field headers as UInt32 byte counts.

\end{fulllineitems}



\paragraph{Finite\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional models}
\label{\detokenize{scrimp.examples:finite-dimensional-models}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Mass\textendash{}spring\textendash{}damper: a finite\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional port\sphinxhyphen{}Hamiltonian example.
\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{State x=(q,p), with displacement q and momentum p=m*q\_dot.}
\sphinxAtStartPar
H(q,p) = k*q**2/2 + p**2/(2*m)
e\_q = dH/dq = k*q,  e\_p = dH/dp = p/m
q\_dot = e\_p
p\_dot = \sphinxhyphen{}e\_q \sphinxhyphen{} c*e\_p + f(t)

\end{description}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Power balance: H\_dot = \sphinxhyphen{}c*e\_p**2 + f*e\_p.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each lumped port has a \sphinxstylestrong{single} DOF. The interval used here is only
a normalization domain for GetFEM’s weak\sphinxhyphen{}form assembly; it is NOT a
spatial discretization of the oscillator.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Nonlinear damped pendulum, modeled as a lumped port\sphinxhyphen{}Hamiltonian system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
States are the angle theta (radians) and angular momentum p = I*theta\_dot.
For a point mass m at distance L from the pivot, the governing
relationships are:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{I} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{m}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}
\PYG{n}{H} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{p}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{I}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{o}{+} \PYG{n}{m}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{g}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{cos}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{theta}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{e\PYGZus{}theta} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{m}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{g}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{sin}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{theta}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}  \PYG{n}{e\PYGZus{}p} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{p}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{I}
\PYG{n}{theta\PYGZus{}dot} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{e\PYGZus{}p}
\PYG{n}{p\PYGZus{}dot} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{e\PYGZus{}theta} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}} \PYG{n}{damping}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{e\PYGZus{}p} \PYG{o}{+} \PYG{n}{tau}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{t}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This example keeps the full nonlinear sine restoring torque. It does
not use the small\sphinxhyphen{}angle approximation sin(theta) = theta.

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{scrimp.utils:scrimp.utils.linalg.convert_gmm_to_petsc}}
\pysigstartsignatures
\pysiglinewithargsret
{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scrimp.utils.linalg.}}\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{convert\_gmm\_to\_petsc}}}
{\sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{M}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{B}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{comm}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{petsc4py.PETSc.COMM\_WORLD}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{keyword-only-separator}{\DUrole{o}{\sphinxstyleabbreviation{*}}}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{profiler}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{None}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{profile\_label}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{None}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{distributed\_coo\_eligible}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{True}}}
{}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Transfer GetFEM’s globally numbered matrix into distributed PETSc.

\sphinxAtStartPar
SCRIMP\_GETFEM\_MATRIX\_MODE selects ASSEMBLY SEMANTICS:
\sphinxhyphen{} replicated: insert owned PETSc rows once (INSERT\_VALUES).
\sphinxhyphen{} distributed: sum all global contributions (ADD\_VALUES).

\sphinxAtStartPar
SCRIMP\_GETFEM\_BRIDGE\_REPLICATED controls only extraction in
replicated mode: ‘full’ (default) or experimental ‘owned\_rows’.

\sphinxAtStartPar
With distributed GetFEM assembly, all production matrix transfers
default to PETSc’s native COO preallocation/assembly, including the
state\sphinxhyphen{}dependent nonlinear mass and stiffness tangents. The GetFEM
contributions may change sparsity between Newton iterations:
setPreallocationCOO is rerun for EACH assembly before setValuesCOO,
using the SAME PETSc Mat handle (not a new Mat per iteration).
The owned structural diagonal is always retained.

\sphinxAtStartPar
SCRIMP\_GETFEM\_BRIDGE\_DISTRIBUTED=csr or ijv remains an EXPLICIT
historical diagnostic override for source\sphinxhyphen{}era benchmark parity;
it is no longer a production default or the nonlinear assembly path.
Replicated GetFEM extraction is retained for serial compatibility.
PETSc stores the assembled sparse matrix as AIJ (CSR\sphinxhyphen{}like):
COO is the assembly API, not the storage format.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The native\sphinxhyphen{}MPI benchmark and complete acoustic trajectory tests
cover 1/2/4/6 ranks and three\sphinxhyphen{}repeat runs for linear operators.
Preservation of the PETSc Mat handle and explicit diagonal slots
is required. Nonlinear COO is NOT enabled without separate tests.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Optional profiler/profile\_label use SCRIMP’s existing TimingProfiler
for bridge subphases. No MPI collectives or matrix changes are added.
The bridge total is already measured by the DPHS assembly methods.

\end{fulllineitems}

\subsubsection{scrimp.sandbox}
\label{\detokenize{scrimp.sandbox:scrimp-sandbox}}\label{\detokenize{scrimp.sandbox::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sandbox}} folder is the \sphinxstylestrong{recommanded} folder to work in.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It already contains the example of the 1D wave equation presented \sphinxhref{started}{here}.


\paragraph{Experimental PDE\textendash{}ODE coupling}
\label{\detokenize{scrimp.sandbox:experimental-pde-ode-coupling}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The sandbox also contains an experimental coupled shallow\sphinxhyphen{}water /
moving\sphinxhyphen{}tank system at \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sandbox/sloshing\_tank.py}} and a convergence
driver at \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sandbox/tank\_convergence.py}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These models demonstrate global scalar ports coupled to distributed
states. The wall boundary conditions and spatial\sphinxhyphen{}field convergence
remain under investigation. The tank example is intentionally \sphinxstylestrong{not}
a release\sphinxhyphen{}validated example yet. See \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sandbox/README\_lumped\_tank.md}}.

\index{assemble\_rhs() (scrimp.dphs.DPHS method)@\spxentry{assemble\_rhs()}\spxextra{scrimp.dphs.DPHS method}}

\begin{fulllineitems}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{scrimp:scrimp.dphs.DPHS.assemble_rhs}}
\pysigstartsignatures
\pysiglinewithargsret
{\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{assemble\_rhs}}}
{\sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{source\_only}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{False}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{explicit\_only}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{False}}}
{}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Assemble the GetFEM RHS into the owned PETSc entries.

\sphinxAtStartPar
GetFEM’s model.rhs() mixes two DIFFERENT signs:
* generic nonlinear weak terms N(z): rhs = \sphinxhyphen{}N(z);
* add\_source\_term\_brick prescribed forcing S(t): rhs = +S(t).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For raw GetFEM rhs\_total=\sphinxhyphen{}P*N(z)+S(t), a generic RHS scale
alpha=1/P alone incorrectly scales the source S/P. The tested
GetFEM MPI\sphinxhyphen{}2 build treats generic terms and source bricks
differently. Opt\sphinxhyphen{}in SCRIMP\_GETFEM\_SOURCE\_RHS\_MODE=raw inserts
unscaled source\sphinxhyphen{}only RHS and reconstructs the direct residual as
\sphinxhyphen{}alpha*rhs\_total + (1+alpha)*rhs\_source = N(z)+S(t).
match\_generic (default) preserves historical uniform scaling.
This flag only affects source bricks’ contribution to the
direct nonlinear residual, not the physical equations or LU.
See sandbox/check\_mcss\_source\_sign.py.

\end{fulllineitems}

\index{init\_step() (scrimp.dphs.DPHS method)@\spxentry{init\_step()}\spxextra{scrimp.dphs.DPHS method}}

\begin{fulllineitems}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{scrimp:scrimp.dphs.DPHS.init_step}}
\pysigstartsignatures
\pysiglinewithargsret
{\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{init\_step}}}
{}
{}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Establish a DAE\sphinxhyphen{}consistent physical initial state.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The v1.3.0 default candidate \sphinxtitleref{algebraic} projects only
algebraic variables while preserving prescribed differential
initial coefficients. It is linear\sphinxhyphen{}only; unsupported or
inconsistent initial data raise explicit errors.
Historical \sphinxtitleref{pseudo} remains available by explicit request;
it integrates a tiny pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}time PETSc TS and can move the
differential coefficients. The alternative historical
\sphinxtitleref{bdf} also uses a short time integration, optionally from a
negative initial time with \sphinxtitleref{init\_step\_bdf\_order=2} and
\sphinxtitleref{init\_step\_from\_negative\_time=True}. PETSc BDF2 bootstraps
its history internally with a half\sphinxhyphen{}step (PETSc 3.21).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxtitleref{init\_step\_ts\_type=algebraic} directly projects only
algebraic variables with a distributed PETSc LSQR solve, and
performs no pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}time integration. Explicit historical
relaxation options remain available. Changing the default
is subject to an independent native and migration release gate;
the main physical TS remains unchanged.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See docs/V130\_DAE\_ALGEBRAIC\_INITIALIZER\_DESIGN.md.

\end{fulllineitems}

{\sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{path}}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Stage a verified full DAE state for a new, cold PETSc CN solve.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Call after building the identical FE model and before solve().
Sets absolute physical t\_0 from checkpoint, forces init\_step=false
(no pseudo/BDF or algebraic consistency reinitialization), then
rechecks original full GetFEM algebraic equations after assembly.
The future physical boundary law must be the SAME as the saved
model. Collective on all MPI ranks. Returns checkpoint metadata.

\end{fulllineitems}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Visualize \sphinxstylestrong{genuine} Hamiltonian terms and cumulative port work.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A primary user\sphinxhyphen{}facing SCRIMP method: no approximation is made
to GetFEM energy integrals, and every rank participates in any
GetFEM/MPI assembly. Only rank0 writes shared figures and data.


\subsubsection{Parameters}
\label{\detokenize{scrimp:id1}}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{with\_powers}{[}bool{]}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Integrate computed algebraic port powers with the sampling
convention of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{actual PETSc TS history}. CN step work
is exact at the specified accepted grid when consecutive
states are stored; subsampled CN and BDF/other schemes
carry an explicit approximate nodal\sphinxhyphen{}trapezoid label.
This is \sphinxstylestrong{not} automatically a model\sphinxhyphen{}independent exact
Hamiltonian power identity.

\sphinxlineitem{save\_figure}{[}bool{]}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Write PNG and SVG figures. Without a configured output
directory, preserve legacy outputs/png/\textless{}filename\textgreater{} and
use outputs/svg/\textless{}stem\textgreater{}.svg for the additional vector plot.

\sphinxlineitem{filename}{[}str{]}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Basename ending in ‘.png’ or ‘.svg’. Either extension
results in both format\sphinxhyphen{}specific files when saved.

\sphinxlineitem{show}{[}bool{]}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Display the Matplotlib figure on rank0 (legacy default).
Set False in batch/native tests to avoid a GUI dependency.

\sphinxlineitem{save\_data}{[}bool{]}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When saving a figure, also write a compressed NPZ with the
true accepted time grid, full Hamiltonian and separate
terms plus the genuine sampled raw port powers.

\end{description}

\end{fulllineitems}

The numerical quadrature follows each Port’s declared
get\_power\_sampling() convention: ‘cn\_step’ integrates original
step powers P{[}k\textgreater{}=1{]} as sum(dt{[}k{]}*P{[}k{]}), never reusing
instantaneous P{[}0{]}; ‘instantaneous’ integrates actual nodal
P(t{[}k{]},z{[}k{]}) with a trapezoidal \sphinxstyleemphasis{approximation}. An unknown
convention fails explicitly, preventing a silent wrong plot.

\sphinxAtStartPar
CN is already native\sphinxhyphen{}qualified for the tested mixed\sphinxhyphen{}boundary
wave; exact BDF/ARKIMEX stage quadrature is NOT claimed
without the underlying PETSc internal\sphinxhyphen{}stage data. Port signs
are the original raw flow\sphinxhyphen{}effort orientation.

sign convention; its constancy is model\sphinxhyphen{}dependent.

Save a complete accepted final state for a later COLD restart.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only supported for completed, accepted PETSc TSCN simulations.
Includes differential and algebraic GetFEM variables and the
absolute physical time. The file is atomic and never overwritten.
This is NOT a snapshot of PETSc TS/KSP/MUMPS or BDF history.

{}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Set a prescribed open\sphinxhyphen{}loop input or an implicit feedback law.

\sphinxAtStartPar
State\sphinxhyphen{}independent GWFL expressions use an RHS\sphinxhyphen{}only GetFEM source.
A bare signed model variable (e.g. Y\_w or \sphinxhyphen{}Y\_T) is
a provably linear feedback: GetFEM assembles its constant
bilinear coupling directly into the stiffness matrix.
A finite numeric scalar times a single model variable
(e.g. \sphinxhyphen{}0.5*Y) is likewise certified linear. Other
state\sphinxhyphen{}dependent expressions, or unknown macros,
use a nonlinear variational brick so Newton computes
their full derivative, not merely the residual.
\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Args:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
name (str): the name of the control port
expression (str): GWFL scalar/vector/tensor expression

\end{description}

\end{fulllineitems}

Flag state\sphinxhyphen{}dependent mass/stiffness terms for reassembly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
GetFEM source bricks contribute only to the RHS, even when
declared linear=False for their special assembly route.
Feedback controls created by set\_control() are \sphinxstyleemphasis{not} sources:
signed bare\sphinxhyphen{}variable feedback is a constant linear coupling
assembled in K; general feedback has a state\sphinxhyphen{}dependent
constitutive tangent and is reassembled per Newton iterate.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Sample all Hamiltonian terms on real accepted FE states/times.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Uses the same real GetFEM generic weak\sphinxhyphen{}form integrals as the
historical implementation. Crucially, set the model time before
each assembly (a Hamiltonian may contain t\sphinxhyphen{}dependent parameters)
and replace, rather than append, previously sampled histories.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each term’s published values are updated only if the full
calculation succeeds. Recomputing twice is numerically idempotent
and cannot silently double the length of its trace.

\end{fulllineitems}

\pysiglinewithargsret

{\sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{solution}\DUrole{p}{:}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{n}{dict}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{gf\_model}\DUrole{p}{:}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{n}{getfem.Model}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{domain}\DUrole{p}{:}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{n}{{\hyperref[\detokenize{scrimp:scrimp.domain.Domain}]{\sphinxcrossref{Domain}}}}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{keyword-only-separator}{\DUrole{o}{\sphinxstyleabbreviation{*}}}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{sampling}\DUrole{p}{:}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{n}{str}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{default_value}{\textquotesingle{}instantaneous\textquotesingle{}}}}
{}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute raw signed flow/effort powers for an algebraic port.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Sampling is explicit rather than hardcoding Crank\textendash{}Nicolson for
every PETSc time integrator:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxtitleref{instantaneous}: at every accepted (t{[}k{]}, z{[}k{]}), suitable as
nodal \sphinxstyleemphasis{samples} independent of the time scheme. Trapezoidal
integration of these samples is approximate and not a claim
of BDF/ARKIMEX stage quadrature or a power identity.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxtitleref{cn\_step}: at (t{[}0{]}, z{[}0{]}) for k=0; for k\textgreater{}=1, evaluate
at (t{[}k{]}, 0.5*(z{[}k\sphinxhyphen{}1{]}+z{[}k{]})), preserving the already\sphinxhyphen{}native\sphinxhyphen{}
qualified SCRIMP CN convention exactly. In particular,
time\sphinxhyphen{}dependent GetFEM expressions are evaluated at t{[}k{]} as
they were historically, \sphinxstylestrong{not} at the physical midpoint time.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{solution}} \textendash{} Accepted time/FE\sphinxhyphen{}state history, containing
matching \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{t}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{z}} sequences.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{gf\_model}} \textendash{} Original GetFEM model (collective MPI assembly).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{domain}} \textendash{} SCRIMP integration domain.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{sampling}} \textendash{} \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{instantaneous}} (default) or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cn\_step}}.

\end{itemize}

\end{description}\end{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The returned \sphinxtitleref{get\_power()} array preserves the original port
algebraic orientation. \sphinxtitleref{get\_power\_sampling()} identifies the
numerical meaning of each stored value.

\end{fulllineitems}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a finite element for a SCRIMP state or port.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Families: CG, DG, RT, BDM, NED1 (Nedelec first kind),
NED2 (Nedelec second kind). The longer names NEDELEC1 and
NEDELEC2 are accepted aliases. Here ‘order’ is the polynomial
index k, \sphinxstylestrong{not} the Nedelec family number. NED2 supports only
k=1,2 in the pinned SCRIMP GetFEM 5.5 patch.
Passing a negative order with an explicit GetFEM descriptor
remains supported for expert/custom elements.

\section{Third\sphinxhyphen{}party}
\label{\detokenize{index:third-party}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The two \sphinxstylestrong{main} libraries used as core for SCRIMP are:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://getfem.org/}{GetFEM} \textendash{} An open\sphinxhyphen{}source finite element library

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://petsc.org/release/}{PETSc} \textendash{} The Portable, Extensible Toolkit for Scientific Computation

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Meshing is facilitated using (although not mandatory) \sphinxhref{https://gmsh.info/}{GMSH} \textendash{} A three\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional finite element mesh generator

\sphinxAtStartPar
Post\sphinxhyphen{}processing visualization is encouraged via \sphinxhref{https://www.paraview.org/}{ParaView} \textendash{} Post\sphinxhyphen{}processing visualization engine

\sphinxAtStartPar
and finally, SCRIMP also needs for some routines
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://matplotlib.org/}{matplotlib} \textendash{} Visualization with Python

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://numpy.org/}{numpy} \textendash{} A well\sphinxhyphen{}known package for scientific computing

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
One of our choice for IDE is \sphinxhref{https://www.spyder-ide.org/}{Spyder} \textendash{} A scientific Python development environment
